articles.title: Russia’s Hybrid War Has Entered a Dangerous New Phase
articles.summary: Julianne Smith, who represented the United States at NATO during the Biden administration, argues that Russian hybrid warfare in Europe is escalating quickly, and NATO is not doing enough to deter it. Putin is attempting to discourage support for Ukraine and undermine faith in Article 5, and NATO is responding with an outdated playbook.
articles.full_text:
For the first few years of the war in Ukraine, Russia’s hybrid warfare attacks in Europe remained just below the threshold that might trigger a collective response. As the United States’ permanent representative to NATO from 2021 to 2024, I watched the campaign develop: undersea cables cut, incendiary devices hidden in cargo packages, and arson attacks on weapons factories and depots across Europe. To address the threat, allies reinforced critical infrastructure, increased patrols in the Baltic Sea, and expanded intelligence sharing. But NATO’s approach remained largely defensive: these attacks were scattered, small in scale, and just deniable enough that Moscow could wave them away.
Today, that is no longer the case. In late July, a Russian cruise missile crashed into Polish territory. Days later, three explosive-laden drones were found at and near an airport in Leipzig, Germany. Two weeks after that, Romanian F-16s scrambled to intercept three Russian drones over Romanian airspace, and a Spanish jet shot down a fourth near the Moldovan border. If someone had described this state of affairs two years ago as where NATO would be now—drones over allied airspace, a Russian cruise missile in Polish territory, explosives at a German airport—without any meaningful collective response from the alliance, it would have sounded unbelievable.
There is little ambiguity about Russian President Vladimir Putin’s aims. These attacks are designed to fracture the alliance’s unity, test the strength of members’ commitment to Article 5—the principle that an attack on one member is an attack on all—and raise the cost of supporting Ukraine. Less expected, however, has been the speed with which his deniable campaign has become undeniable.
NATO has not looked away. The alliance tracks these incidents, investigates them, and sometimes intercepts attacks. But a response built incident by incident is not deterrence, and Putin knows the difference. As long as each provocation costs Moscow nothing more than a downed drone, Putin has every reason to keep escalating. And every escalation in turn increases the risk that one of these incidents will end in catastrophic loss of life. Mobilizing collective action to impose costs is the best chance the alliance has of preventing such a scenario.
MASK OFF
For Russia, hybrid tactics are far from a new tradecraft. As early as the 1920s and continuing throughout the Cold War, the Soviets relied on what they called “active measures”: the use of local proxies, front groups, and irregular forces to achieve political aims. Today, Putin follows essentially the same model, seeking to erode allies’ confidence in NATO’s Article 5 by relying on tactics that fall below the threshold of a conventional warfare and leave unaffected members hesitant to respond. Plausible deniability has always been a critical part of these operations. Whatever the method, whether it be severing undersea fiber-optic cables in the Baltic Sea, a coordinated cyberattack, or an explosion at a plant in eastern Europe that produces artillery shells for Ukraine, Russia is quick to deny its direct involvement. Often, it flips the script, accusing NATO members of “Russophobia” and directing blame at Ukrainian or rogue actors.
NATO members have long been familiar with this Russian playbook. Most European members have experienced multiple hybrid attacks over the past two decades. But since its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Russia has changed its strategy in two meaningful ways. First, it has significantly increased the frequency of attacks; during the first year of the war, the number of Russian incursions in Europe quadrupled, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies. It has also diversified its tactics. In addition to familiar disinformation campaigns, airspace violations, and cyberattacks, actors linked to Moscow have sabotaged railways, placed incendiary packages on cargo planes, and paid criminal networks inside Europe to burn down weapons depots.
By early 2023, in response to these trends, NATO stepped up the seriousness and urgency of its discussions on Russian hybrid activity. The 2023 NATO summit’s communiqué, which sets out the alliance’s shared positions and priorities, stated that Russia had “intensified” its attacks against allies and mentioned Russia’s use of proxies for the first time. The alliance also rolled out an array of new initiatives to counter hybrid activity: heads of state adopted new goals for protecting critical infrastructure and supply chains from strategic shocks across alliance territory. They also agreed to establish the NATO Maritime Centre for the Security of Critical Undersea Infrastructure and the Virtual Cyber Incident Support Capability, a coordination platform to help members respond to cyberattacks. What was missing was any measure to impose costs on Russia. Although NATO condemned Moscow’s hybrid warfare, it was not prepared to talk explicitly about consequences, such as targeted sanctions, a crackdown on Russia’s shadow fleet (the unmarked vessels Russia uses to bypass sanctions), offensive cyber-activities, or information operations.
 In late 2025, Putin put his hybrid war into overdrive. 
Part of the problem is structural. NATO was established and designed, in 1949, for collective defense against attributable armed attacks. It was not designed to impose costs after deniable acts. As a defensive military alliance, it lacks the authority to impose sanctions or expel Russian operatives from member countries. That power sits with individual member states and the European Union. Since its 2014 summit, NATO has maintained that a cyber or hybrid attack could trigger Article 5 on a “case by case basis,” but the alliance has never defined the threshold for action. Even in cases in which the alliance could act collectively, such as through offensive cyber-operations, doing so requires consensus among 32 countries that have very different histories, domestic politics, and appetites for risk.
In the year after the 2023 NATO summit, Russia continued to turn up the heat, tripling its hybrid attacks in Europe and testing new ways to target NATO territory, such as interference with European railway systems. Consequently, the alliance improved its detection, forensics, and response options. NATO members shared best practices, participated in tabletop exercises designed to test those options, and crafted a new strategy to counter disinformation. Many countries, such as Estonia, Germany, Poland, and the United Kingdom, independently opened investigations into, sought prosecutions of, and expelled Russian diplomats and suspected intelligence officers. These steps were important. But they were not enough to deter Russia.
In 2025, hopes for further NATO action stalled. When President Donald Trump returned to the White House, he was so intent on getting NATO members to spend more on defense that virtually every engagement with allies began and ended with that single issue. Such ruthless prioritization produced some admirable results. At the 2025 NATO summit at The Hague, all allies committed to spend five percent of GDP on defense by 2035. But instead of taking the win and directing the alliance’s attention back toward Russia’s hybrid warfare, the administration continued to badger allies to spend more and faster. When I visited NATO headquarters in November 2025 and asked former colleagues how they were spending their time, one country’s permanent representative answered, “We spend most of our time managing you.” Amid this upheaval, the alliance’s momentum on hybrid warfare slowed to a crawl. Despite an agreement among allies in 2024 to deliver a new Russia strategy at the 2025 summit at The Hague, it never materialized. The summit declaration didn’t even mention Russia’s hybrid war.
FROG IN A POT
The summer of 2025 seemed to mark a high point for Putin’s confidence. In addition to NATO’s waning focus on hybrid activity, Russia’s summer offensive in Ukraine was showing signs of success, NATO allies were bickering over tariffs and whether Europe was facing what Vice President JD Vance called “civilizational suicide,” and Putin was being courted by Trump, a dynamic on public display in a U.S.-Russian summit in Alaska in August.
By September 2025, Putin no longer seemed to care as much about plausible deniability, and Russia’s hybrid war campaign became increasingly brazen. That month, around 20 Russian drones entered Polish airspace, and three Russian fighter jets crossed into Estonian airspace before being shot down and chased out, respectively, by NATO forces. After each instance, NATO convened for Article 4 consultations, which, according to the treaty, take place when “the territorial integrity, political independence or security of any of the Parties is threatened.” NATO launched “Eastern Sentry,” an initiative to increase NATO’s vigilance over the alliance’s eastern flank with no set end date. The initiative placed additional allied air and counterdrone assets under NATO command to reinforce its existing integrated air and missile defense along that border. Although a much-needed addition to NATO’s efforts to combat hybrid warfare, this step also failed to deter Russian attacks.
 NATO needs to mount a more forceful response to Moscow’s escalation.

Q1. As you know, the Republic of South Africa brought a case before the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in 2023 on the grounds that Israel had violated the international Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. As an academic and activist who has worked in the field of international law for many years, what did you think of the ICJ decision? Who will be responsible for implementing the decision on the ground? Have those responsible taken action on the ground? How should international law be mobilized on the ground? Or are we to say that the UN’s highest judicial organ is ineffective?
R1. In what may yet become the most important judicial initiative in the 81 year history of ICJ, due to the gravity and visibility of the South African submissions charging violations of the Genocide Convention in December 2023. To date the court has only rendered a series of preliminary decisions in 2024 on Interim Measures involving requests by South Africa that Israel be ordered to stop its assault on Gaza and an emergency is unfolding. The majority opinion of the ICJ agreed that the combat tactics during the first five month after the October 7th by Israel constituted ‘a plausible genocide’ that should be paused pending a final decision and that Israel must immediatelu stop its interference with the delivery of humanitarian aid so that it can reach the 2.3 million civilian population of Gaza. These ICJ rulings were viewed enthusiastically throughout the world except of course for Israel and its complicit North American and European supporters.
As anticipated, Israel defied these Interim Measures, and nothing effective could be done to implement the ICJ decisions on the ground at the UN or elsewhere. In the absence of voluntary compliance with its rulings, the ICJ is dependent for enforcement upon a veto-free süper-majority vote of 9 affirmative votes of the 15 states in the UN Security Council. It is also controversially possible for the imposition of national sanctions by Member states to function as a supplemental enforcement mechanisms. Neither mode of enforcement was forthcoming in this crucial situation. We can conclude that the ICJ is only effective if none of the five permanent members of the Security Council invokes its right of veto or if these states, the major winners of World War II who were given managerial control over the implementation of international law in global situations as embodied in the UN Charter approach to ICJ enforcement.
From the Gaza experience it should not be concluded that the ICJ is entirely ineffective. Its judgments in high-profile litigation of this sort can exert a strong influence on public discourse and stimulate protest activity in çivil society worldwide. Such was the impact of the first of the Interim Measure ICJ decisions. Many influential media platforms also responded by tending to offer somewhat more balanced coverage of the daily happenings in Gaza, street and campus demonstrations spread, and the taboo on describing the violence as genocide was greatly weakened if not altogether abandoned. These pro-Palestinian developments are partially attributable to the legitimacy accorded to the legality of outcomes at the ICJ regardless of whether the losing side complies or the UN enforces.
A final point: it is a mistake to regard international law in its totality as ineffective because of its failures in the all-important war and genocide prevention contexts. In many routine yet vital transnational settings of international law works without regard to the inequality of political actors. International law provides reliability through compliance in such settings as respect for diplomatic immunity, air and maritime safety, tourism, freedom of navigation on the high seas, that is, in relation to behavior regulated by the win/win logic of reciprocity rather than the win/lose logic of power.
Q2. In our interview in October 2024 (https://perspektif.online/tufandan-sonra-askeri-ve-jeopolitik-kirilmanin-ilk-yili/), you said, “The US’s support for Israel at the expense of disregarding international law is an example of moral hypocrisy.” Does this moral hypocrisy also apply to Europe? Can we say that the Gaza Genocide has destroyed the West’s claim to moral superiority?
R2. Yes, more so than in 2024 the comparison between the outrage over the Russian attack on Ukraine and undisguised complicity in the most tramsparent genocide perpetrated by Israel in Gaza, undermines the authority of international law in the context of issues of global security. International law shifts its functionality from being a regulative process applicable to all sovereign states to being a policy instrument useful to mount state propaganda against adversaries but to be disregarded and circumvented when it involves strategic allies.
Europe has certainly joined the U.S., Canada, and Australia in closing ranks both with respect to denouncing the unlawfulness of Russia’s behavior in Ukraine while supporting the genocidal assault by Israel in Gaza. In relation to both of these conflicts NATO solidarity unified Atlanticist responses. This solidarity fractured to some extent in relation to the second Iran War of 2026.
Q3. In some of your articles and books that I reviewed, beginning in the 1970s and continuing through 2008, I came across the following titles: The Status of Law in International Society, The Future of the International Legal Order, International Law and World Order, International Law, the UN and World Order after Iraq. My question is this: Is there still such a norm as International Law? If the international legal order has become dysfunctional following the Gaza Genocide and Israel’s unlawful occupation and attacks against regional countries in the Middle East such as Lebanon, Iran, and Syria, what should take its place?

I was part of the post-1945 generation that worried above all about the dangers of an apocalyptic nuclear war that would have catastrophic effects on the future of humanity. I hoped that humane rationality would prevail over the type of ‘political realism’ that operated as a hegemonic ideology in the inner circles of foreign policy decision-making.
I was greatly influenced by the U.S. involvement in the Vietnam War both for reasons of compliance with law and morality, and by the existential experience of witnessing first-hand the cruelty and onesidedness of a high-tech military superpower devastating a vulnerable, poorly developed society in Global South with no means of retaliation. I also saw that despite this unchallenged military superiority of the United States, it managed to lose the war, allowing a victimized people to achieve their goals of decolonization, national liberation, and self-determination. articles.full_text:
Bulgarian authorities have ended search operations after confirming no survivors were found following a drone strike that sank a ship off the country’s coast.
Drones hit two commercial vessels early on Tuesday as attacks on Black Sea shipping increase amid an intensifying Russia-Ukraine war. One caught fire, and the other sank.
“There is no trace of the sailors,” Rumen Nikolov, the head of the country’s Maritime Search and Rescue Coordination Centre, told reporters on Wednesday.
The search stopped late on Tuesday and would not continue, he added.
Eighteen Turkish and Indian crew members were rescued from the ship that caught fire, but the crew members from the vessel that sank remain missing.
Authorities have not said how many people are missing, but according to the Maritime.bg specialised website, 10 people were on board the ship.
Nikolov said the incident occurred in a so-called “responsible search and rescue zone” and not in the country’s territorial waters, which extend to 12 nautical miles off the coast.
“What was found from the sunken ship was one overturned boat, three life rafts and debris from the ship’s equipment that was floating on the surface of the sea,” he said.
Asked whether any debris from the drones had been recovered, Nikolov said: “I have no information about drone debris.”
Prime Minister Rumen Radev has described the attack as “absolutely unacceptable”.
European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen has also condemned the incident.
Bulgarian authorities have said they are not yet able to determine the origin of the drones.
A distress beacon signal from the ship that sank was received at 2:54am on Tuesday (23:54 GMT on Monday), while the distress signal from the other ship was received at 3:23am (00:23 GMT), Nikolov said.
Both commercial ships were managed by Turkiye-based companies, according to the Equasis merchant shipping database.
They were hit about 80 nautical miles (150km) east of the Bulgarian coastal town of Byala.
The strikes came a day after another ship caught fire and sank off the Romanian coast on Monday, killing two people. Ukraine blamed Russia for the drone attack.

articles.title: Why Has Yemen’s War Escalated Again and What Does It Mean for the Red Sea? - Modern Diplomacy
articles.summary: Why Has Yemen’s War Escalated Again and What Does It Mean for the Red Sea?  Modern Diplomacy
articles.full_text:
Yemen’s long-running war has entered another dangerous phase, with Houthi missile and drone attacks on airports in southern Yemen and Saudi Arabia coinciding with a government counter-offensive along the country’s strategically important Red Sea coast.
The escalation threatens to reopen one of the Middle East’s most complex conflicts after years of relative calm and could have consequences well beyond Yemen. The fighting is unfolding around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints, while also drawing Saudi Arabia and Iran deeper into a renewed regional confrontation.
The latest escalation began after Yemeni government forces, backed by Saudi-led coalition air power, launched a rapid counter-offensive against the Iran-aligned Houthis.
Government forces say they have retaken territory captured by the Houthis last month, including areas along the Red Sea coast near the strategic city of Mocha and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Houthis responded on Wednesday by targeting Aden International Airport with ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones, according to Yemen’s Transport Ministry.
One missile landed near the runway shortly before a flight from Cairo was scheduled to arrive. The flight was diverted to Jeddah, while aircraft already on the ground were moved away from the area because of concerns about further attacks.
Aden is the principal international gateway for areas of Yemen outside Houthi control, making an attack on its airport particularly significant for civilian travel and humanitarian access.
Why Has the Fighting Intensified?
The immediate trigger is the government-backed military campaign to reclaim territory from the Houthis.
The offensive is targeting the Red Sea coast, including areas around Mocha and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Control of this territory is strategically important because the strait connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and serves as a major route for international shipping.
The Houthis have responded by expanding their attacks beyond the immediate battlefield.
The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile north of Riyadh. Saudi authorities said they were also tracking the launch platform in Houthi-controlled Sanaa.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree separately claimed that the group had targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with several drones.
The Houthis also claimed attacks against Abha International Airport and a military airbase in the southwestern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait.
Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm all of the reported attacks, making the full scale of the escalation difficult to establish.
Nevertheless, the geography of the reported strikes shows how quickly renewed fighting inside Yemen can expand into a wider regional security problem.
Yemen’s War Has Never Truly Been Resolved
The current escalation is a reminder that Yemen’s conflict was never permanently settled.
The Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014, prompting Saudi Arabia and its allies to intervene militarily the following year. Riyadh viewed the expansion of the group as a major security threat and as evidence of growing Iranian influence on its southern border.
The conflict subsequently developed into a prolonged war involving multiple Yemeni factions and external powers.
A UN-brokered truce in 2022 significantly reduced large-scale fighting but failed to produce a comprehensive political settlement.
The result was an unstable pause rather than a durable peace.
The latest fighting suggests that the underlying disputes over territorial control, political authority and regional influence remain unresolved.
Why Is the Red Sea So Important?
The renewed fighting around the Red Sea coast carries significance beyond Yemen because of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The narrow waterway is a critical connection between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. Any sustained threat to shipping through the area can increase transportation costs, disrupt supply chains and force commercial vessels to take longer routes around Africa.
The Houthis have previously demonstrated their ability to use missiles and drones to threaten regional targets and shipping.
Their ability to strike both Yemeni territory and locations inside Saudi Arabia means the conflict could once again become a wider security challenge for the Gulf and international maritime trade.
The possibility of attacks around the Bab el-Mandeb is particularly sensitive because the region has already experienced major disruptions to shipping in recent years.
Where Does Iran Fit In?
Iran remains central to the regional dimension of the conflict.
Saudi Arabia and its allies accuse Tehran of providing the Houthis with weapons, training and financial support. The Houthis reject the description of themselves as an Iranian proxy and maintain that they develop their own military capabilities.
Iran has also denied the allegations.
Nevertheless, the Houthis’ missile and drone capabilities have made them one of the most significant armed actors in the region.
Their ability to threaten Saudi territory and potentially disrupt maritime traffic gives Tehran and its regional partners an additional source of leverage during periods of heightened confrontation.
The latest escalation is therefore taking place against a broader backdrop of tensions between Iran and its regional rivals.
What Happens Next?
The most immediate concern is whether the current counter-offensive remains limited or develops into a much broader campaign.
If government forces continue advancing along the Red Sea coast, the Houthis could intensify missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia and government-held areas. That could draw the Saudi-led coalition into deeper military involvement and increase the risk of civilian casualties.
A prolonged offensive could also threaten the fragile political balance created by the 2022 truce.
For Saudi Arabia, the priority will be preventing renewed Houthi attacks from becoming a sustained threat to its territory and critical infrastructure. For the Yemeni government, the offensive presents an opportunity to regain territory and strengthen its negotiating position.
For the Houthis, maintaining control over large parts of northern Yemen remains essential to their political and military survival.
The wider international concern is the possibility that Yemen once again becomes a major front in a broader Middle Eastern confrontation.
The country’s war has repeatedly demonstrated that local territorial disputes can quickly become entangled with competition between regional powers. With fighting now reaching airports and strategically important territory around the Red Sea, the risk is that Yemen’s fragile ceasefire gives way to another prolonged cycle of escalation.
With information from Reuters.

articles.full_text:
Three civilians have been killed and 36 injured in Houthi-claimed attacks on two airports in Saudi Arabia, according to a statement from the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).
Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh were targeted in two separate attacks on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Recommended Stories
The attack on Abha International Airport killed two female residents, a Moroccan and an Algerian, and injured 28 others, GACA reported.
The attack on King Khalid International Airport in the capital Riyadh killed a Sudanese citizen and injured eight residents, including five Saudi citizens.
GACA said it is working “in full integration and continuous coordination with the relevant security authorities” to assess the damage and take all necessary measures to ensure the safety of passengers and workers.
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, Major-General Turki al-Maliki, said forces intercepted a ballistic missile north of Riyadh and destroyed a platform in Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, that had been used to launch attacks on the Saudi capital.
Previous attacks on Saudi airports
New cage-like fences have been erected this week around fuel tanks and other equipment of the Saudi state-run Aramco oil company near the Riyadh airport.
On September 18, Saudi-led coalition forces said they intercepted and destroyed a suspected Houthi ballistic missile fired towards the airport in Riyadh from Yemen.
A day later, on September 19, at least one explosion was heard near the airport in Riyadh, and a large plume of black smoke was seen rising from a fuel storage area at King Khalid International Airport.
Saudi-backed Yemeni forces from the country’s internationally recognised government are locked in escalating combat with Iran-aligned Houthi forces who seized a broad swathe of territory astride the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government said the Houthis launched ballistic missiles and drones against Aden airport early on Wednesday. No casualties were reported.
Meanwhile, the United States embassy in Riyadh has issued another security alert for Americans in Saudi Arabia due to the ongoing security situation, reminding “all US citizens to exercise heightened vigilance”.

“Avoid travel to the island of Djerba on or around Oct. 7, 2026,” the embassy said in a statement.

Djerba, which became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023, has a long history of Jewish settlement dating back nearly 2,000 years, according to the World Jewish Congress.
Thousands of Jewish visitors from around the world travel to Djerba each year to celebrate the Lag B’Omer festival between Passover and Shavuot.

articles.title: British billionaire warned Epstein was a ‘sexual deviant’ decades before FBI closed in on the abuser - The Guardian
articles.summary: British billionaire warned Epstein was a ‘sexual deviant’ decades before FBI closed in on the abuser  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
For Jeffrey Epstein, the billionaire Goldsmith family was a gateway to elite society and he wanted to be in their circle.
The disgraced financier, who died in prison in 2019 facing sex-trafficking charges, longed for a billionaire’s lifestyle and cultivated the family’s friends, bankers, business associates and advisers.
But Sir James Goldsmith, who was knighted by the Queen in 1976 and became a prominent British politician, remained wary of the American financier and even “despised” him, his daughter Jemima recently told the Guardian.
Two decades before Epstein came under federal investigation, Goldsmith – who died in 1997 – told a confidant that Epstein was a “sexual deviant” who was recruiting children for illicit activities.
Goldsmith “told me not to have anything to do with him, that he was a pervert, and he didn’t want him near any of us. He had four daughters to protect,” recalled the famous French architect Robert Couturier, who designed opulent homes for Goldsmith in New York and Mexico.
Goldsmith’s alleged warning came around 1987, years before complaints about Epstein’s solicitation of young girls for sex began filtering into federal law enforcement. Epstein’s network of pretty “girls” evolved into what authorities describe as a global sex-trafficking ring that catered to the ultra-rich and powerful.
It would become a scandal that touched royals, politicians, businessmen, academics, foreign diplomats and celebrities around the world, and left more than 1,000 victims in its wake.
“That is the pity of it all. It was all preventable,” Couturier told the Guardian. Epstein, born on Coney Island, had been on the radar of New York’s elite since he first surfaced at society events, often on the arm of heiresses, Couturier said.
“He was a charmer and a talker. Lots of rich people are deeply gullible, as protected as they are from reality. No one did anything about it.”
In the mid-1980s, Sir James Goldsmith – known as “Jimmy” – announced he was making a shift in his US business operations. Goldsmith had hired a new chief executive who would open an office for him in Hilton Head, South Carolina, an emerging luxury resort.
Goldsmith’s Hilton Head office is rarely mentioned in writings about his reign as the “lucky gambler”, as Time Magazine called him, an adviser to US presidents who became one of the world’s richest men by betting on undervalued companies. His conglomerate, with command centers in Paris and London, had its US headquarters in New York, close to his elegant Manhattan townhouse where Goldsmith entertained and where the young Epstein trolled for wealthy clients.
Hilton Head at the time was undergoing a chaotic development boom that brought in a rush of speculators, shady operators and vacationers lured by star-studded golf tournaments and tennis matches. Its population, 11,000 in 1980, doubled in a decade. Its tiny airport was suddenly a busy landing strip for private jets, including a $10m Gulfstream owned by Goldsmith’s company that was parked there for quick hops.
Epstein developed a lifelong fascination with Goldsmith, his family and fortune, an investigation by the Guardian found.
Epstein’s connection to Goldsmith, and the presence of the billionaire’s company and his associates on a South Carolina sea island – which was attracting an infusion of investors – is potentially relevant because of an alleged sexual assault that is said to have occurred there in the 1980s. A woman known only as Jane Doe 4 claimed in four FBI interviews after Epstein’s 2019 arrest that he had assaulted her during his visits to the island in the 1980s, when she was still a teenager. She has also claimed the man she only knew as “Jeff” trafficked her to other men, including Donald Trump.
The White House has vehemently denied the allegation about the US president, calling it “completely baseless” and “backed by zero credible evidence”.
The Guardian has been examining records, digging into archives and conducting interviews to explore intersections of Goldsmith and Epstein and try to understand if Epstein, with decades of secretive movements and a web of global financial ties, might have had reason to be on Hilton Head in the 1980s when those alleged assaults by Epstein occurred. This remains a mystery, but Epstein’s relationship with Goldsmith provides some additional clues.
Those who dismiss the claim of Jane Doe 4 – including Epstein’s brother Mark – have cited the lack of a public record of his presence on the island as proof that her story is untrue. Mark Epstein told the Guardian he has “no knowledge of him being in Hilton Head”.
Understanding how Epstein won and retained access to power and privilege throughout his life is important as criminal investigations of his sexual abuse and financial crimes continue around the globe. Federal prosecutors in New York have opened an investigation into the two overseers – Darren Indyke and Richard Kahn – of Epstein’s $577m estate, according to the Wall Street Journal. Both have denied they knew of Epstein’s criminal behavior. The Department of Justice has said that Epstein “harmed” over 1,000 people, including minors who were sexually abused.
The justice department has released about 3.5m documents under the Epstein Disclosure Act, including reams of emails, letters and bank transactions. But the trove includes almost no records from the 1980s, leaving a large gap in the public’s understanding. Epstein’s alleged victims continue to accuse the justice department of a cover-up for holding back documents that might implicate Trump and other powerful men in Epstein’s exclusive circle. Trump has said he ended their friendship in 2004 after a real estate dispute and kicked Epstein out of his Mar-A-Lago club in 2007 for poaching employees.
It is unclear whether Goldsmith’s concerns about Epstein stemmed from specific encounters, and there is no indication that Goldsmith ever reported his concerns to local or federal law enforcement.
It took decades for the FBI to catch up with Epstein’s crimes. Federal investigators in Florida charged him in 2008 with soliciting sex from minors after a two-year investigation in which they interviewed young women, including some minors, who he paid for sexual encounters in his Palm Beach mansion. He served 13 months in jail under a lenient deal cut with federal prosecutors.
Until now, the earliest warning about Epstein’s criminal behavior is believed to have come in 1996, when one alleged victim – an artist named Maria Farmer – claims she alerted authorities that she was sexually assaulted by Epstein, according to a lawsuit she has brought against the FBI. Farmer has also claimed that Epstein stole nude images she had of her two minor siblings, which she kept for her personal use in her artwork. The FBI has said in response to the ongoing litigation, which now includes 34 alleged victims, that agents do not have a duty to investigate “every single tip that comes across their desk”.
A fascination with ‘Sir James’
Since Epstein’s death, Goldsmith has been portrayed as an important influence in his early career.
The New York Times last year described Sir James as a connection Epstein shrewdly calculated was “worth nurturing for the long haul”. It recounted a party scene at Goldsmith’s Upper East Side mansion where Epstein, trained in classical piano, serenaded guests with a piano solo from the grand entry hall.
Goldsmith’s warnings about Epstein came just as Epstein signed one of his biggest clients, the Ohio retail magnate Les Wexner, the founder of Victoria’s Secret, who was then ranked by Forbes as the 10th richest person in the US. Wexner says he severed the relationship with Epstein in 2007 after discovering he had stolen funds from Wexner.
Some questions about Epstein and Goldsmith may never be answered given the secrecy surrounding these events and the refusal of key sources to answer questions.
Meanwhile, the debate over the government’s release of the Epstein files rages on. Attorney general Todd Blanche has declined to release about 2.5m Epstein documents he deemed duplicative. An independent journalist, Katie Phang, is suing Blanche to try to force their release, and Blanche recently quietly turned over some of the documents related to Jane Doe 4 to a federal judge, who is reviewing the documents in his chambers.
Prominent figures caught up in the Epstein controversy include former US president Bill Clinton, former Prince Andrew, former Harvard president Larry Summers and billionaire investor Leon Black. Black was recently held in contempt of Congress for his refusal to comply with subpoenas issued to him by the House oversight committee in connection to its Epstein investigation.
Epstein’s emails about the Goldsmiths sometimes suggested bruised feelings and revealed he was watching the family from afar. He was not among the dozens of invited guests in 1997 to Jemima Goldsmith’s grand wedding party to the cricketer-turned-politician Imran Khan, who served as Pakistani prime minister, according to the guest list.
Just before he finished his lenient 2008 sentence for sex crimes in Palm Beach, Epstein scolded a young Romanian admirer for turning down her exclusive invite to a swanky dinner at Jemima’s Oxfordshire estate.
“That was a BIG mistake,” he wrote in an angry 2010 email.
Epstein criticized daughter Jemima’s choice of husband, calling Khan – who is now divorced from Goldsmith and in jail on corruption charges – a “whacko”.
In a 2018 text, Epstein wrote of Imran Khan: “makes donald look like einstein. incapable of truth. , devout islamisist . many nuclear weapons. ( not erdogan or khomeni). he was married to two friends of mine. one daughter of jimmy goldsmith.”
After the family distanced itself from him, Epstein gathered gossip about James’s daughter Isabel’s haughty behavior and joked when a hurricane seemed destined to damage Las Alamandas, her posh Mexican resort.

articles.full_text:
The Under Secretary of War for Policy, Elbridge A. Colby, delivered an update on the Implementation of the National Defense Strategy to the Senate Armed Services Committee. It’s an interesting point by point update on priorities and related actions.
Overall, the National Defense Strategy sets 4 priority objectives, in the order: Defending the US Homeland; deter China in the Indo-Pacific through strength, not confrontation; increase burden sharing with Allies and finally supercharging the US industrial base.
Defence of the Homeland is a wide-ranging objective not at all limited to physical defence of CONUS. The update begins by highlighting the effort to secure the US borders against illegal immigration and drug trafficking. It notes 16 consecutive months of zero releases at the border and a 94% reduction in daily apprehensions from the last Administration. It also notes how homicide rates within major American Cities have dropped by double digits: down 42% in Washington DC, circa 43% in Memphis, 32% in New Orleans and 18% in Los Angeles.
On the back of Operation ABSOLUTE RESOLVE, which led to the apprehension of Nicolas Maduro, “long wanted for his role in trafficking enormous amounts of cocaine to the United States”, the update notes the effects of Op SOUTHERN SPEAR which has resulted in the steady degradation of regional narcotrafficking operations, “driving historic reductions in cocaine shipments through major maritime corridors, including an up to 60 percent reduction in the movement of vessels with US bound cocaine”.
Building on the “Trump Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine”, DoW is investing in building partnerships in the region. The Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (A3C) is mentioned, as an “unprecedented” 19-Nations alliance going on the offense against narcoterrorism networks.
It also underlines efforts to “secure US access to the Panama Canal” through, including through the “reinvigorated” PANAMAX exercises. The 2026 edition was the first held in the field in Panama since 2012 after a long period of “tabletop only” editions. The 11-day event was held in August and saw the participation of elements from multiple A3C countries.
The document also notes “historic partnerships in the Caribbean, namely with Jamaica, the Bahamas, and the Dominican Republic, which will further enable us to protect U.S. commercial and military traffic through the Panama Canal”.
Key to Homeland defence is also the modernization of the Nuclear Forces. The document notes the first “vertical integration of an inert Sentinel missile at Vandenberg Space Force Base to enable flight testing in 2027; a 25 percent increase in B-21 RAIDER production; remaining on track to place aircraft at Ellsworth Air Force Base in 2027; establishment of a dedicated Submarine Launched Cruise Missile-Nuclear program office; and, in coordination with the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA), initiation of a project to adapt a warhead for that capability”. It also notes an ongoing classified review of US nuclear employment guidance “with the goal of increasing options available to the President for purposes of deterring or responding effectively to a nuclear contingency, again in light of the changing global nuclear landscape.”
Next is Golden Dome for America, which is “working toward an integrated demonstration in FY2028, which will encompass GDA’s effectiveness against multiple simultaneous threats, such as various unmanned aerial systems, with the comprehensive suite of kinetic and non-kinetic effectors.”
The document does not expand on Greenland, but this is presumably deliberate as the update was delivered on September 22, the same day when the new Agreement between US, Kingdom of Denmark and Greenland was signed. Presumably it was not the right time to unveil further details fresh out of negotiations.
The ongoing counter terrorism efforts and the conflict against Iran also feed into “Homeland Defense”. The ongoing fight against ISIS has seen the US and Allies finally leave Iraq earlier this month. The US update notes that “we enabled the Iraqi Security Forces to to take the lead in the fight against the remaining ISIS presence in Iraq by transitioning Operation INHERENT RESOLVE’s military mission there and continuing to target ISIS leadership in Syria, most recently with a successful strike on June 19.” Despite the pull-out from Iraq, DoW maintains options to take “focused, decisive action” where needed.
The document notes efforts ongoing in the Africa as well: in Nigeria it mentions the success of Operation GALAVINIC COBRA “which removed ISIS’s second in command and emir for Global Operations, Abu Bilal al-Minuki, his inner circle, and an additional 199 ISIS-West Africa fighters through a deliberate, low-cost, and expeditionary presence”. Operations in Nigeria are meant to address threats “emanating from the Lake Chad Basin”. Work is ongoing alongside Nigerian partners to “improve their existing CT capability to lead efforts to counter regional terrorism threats from ISIS and al-Qaida (AQ) groups that have the intent but not the capability to attack the U.S. homeland – a key burden sharing initiative - and address threats to Christians and other vulnerable communities in the Middlebelt”.
The document also addresses the execution of “over 80 strikes” against Islamic terrorists in Somalia.
The second priority, dealing with China, is of particular interest. It articulates “President Trump’s direction to always negotiate from a position of strength. Therefore, even as we work to avoid confrontation, we continue our efforts to strengthen deterrence by denial along the First Island Chain (FIC)”. The goal, in the words of Secretary Hegseth at the Shangri-La 2026 event, is to ensure that “aggression is infeasible, escalation unattractive, and war deemed irrational.”
In order to achieve this vision, the focus is placed on: Undersea Forces; Long-Range, Long-Endurance air power; Ground-based, mobile, long-range fires; resilient, proliferated space architecture and related counterspace capabilities; Special operations and other stand-in forces; Naval mines and the means to deliver them; relevant integrated air and missile defenses.
Backing all of these if the priority accorded to building “magazine depth, contested logistics capacity, and resilient and cyber-hardened C2”. On the first point in particular, the document notes the unprecedented boost of some 53 billion in the FY2027 budget to increase production and stockpiles of “prioritized munitions”. The “Department recognizes we need both high-end munitions and munitions specifically designed to be rapidly producible in large quantities” and further notes that while critical to the China strategy, stockpiles also enable “options” in other theatres and scenarios, an observation that seems to point the finger against too small reserves of strategic ammunitions exposed by operations against Iran.
On burden-sharing, the document reiterates what the Trump Administration has said from day one: in Europe “the Department has been clear with our NATO allies about what it is that we seek. As Secretary Hegseth said recently, the US is focused on “transforming NATO back into a real military alliance that’s focused on hard power and real deterrence, a NATO 3.0 modeled on the NATO 1.0 that won the Cold War, with our allies actually taking the lead in Europe’s conventional defense.”
The re-balancing of the burden is a “matter of fairness to Americans” but is “also for structural reasons, above all to solve the simultaneity problem, thereby ensuring NATO can defend Europe effectively even in the most trying of circumstances”, in other words when US forces might be busy elsewhere.
The document notes Europe’s progresses and has particularly appreciative words for Germany’s efforts. It goes on to note that with NATO having accepted the “what” the US seek, focus is now on showing Allies “how to step up and then helping them to do so. We are doing so at the bilateral level through technical talks and other higher-level engagements with key allies focused on military strategy and planning, defense industrial cooperation, and other opportunities to work more closely together, such as ongoing exploration of potential opportunities for permanent basing of U.S. forces in Poland. We are also engaging high-performing allies in small-group settings, such as the selective Bergen Group format, thereby accelerating efforts to build coalitions and drive progress toward NATO 3.0.”
The Bergen Group format, which met twice already, the first time in Bergen, Norway (from there comes the name) is due to have a meeting in Poland next month and in these days various Press voices have underlined the exclusion of, most notably, United Kingdom, France and Baltic Countries. This is by design. The Bergen group comprises Norway, Sweden, Finland, Poland, Germany and the Netherlands and might expand to Denmark following the agreement reached on Greenland.
In terms of reductions to US forces permanently earmarked for Europe, “the Department has reduced the total number of manned brigade combat teams (BCTs) assigned or allocated to U.S. European Command from five to three, returning us to the level of BCTs in Europe in 2021. At the Secretary’s direction, we are also undertaking a formal six-month review of U.S. force posture and basing in Europe to ensure that the remaining U.S. presence is appropriately scoped to advance the President’s objectives. The options provided by this Review will be based on strategic rigor, a strong empirical baseline, and a clear sense of the geopolitical and military realities.”
On Ukraine, the document reiterates that “European leadership in support for Ukraine’s defense is not only possible and appropriate but also fully consistent with Ukraine’s ability to defend itself effectively.” It notes that “this has been borne out”, particularly thanks to “allies now covering the costs of U.S.-provided aid to Ukraine vi

articles.summary: Nobel prize in chemistry awarded for work on mirror-image molecules  The GuardianNobel Prize in Chemistry awarded to Kagan and Soai  BBCExplainer: what are autocatalysis and non-linear effects and why have they won the 2026 Nobel prize in chemistry?  Chemistry WorldA Nobel for illuminating life’s asymmetry  The EconomistThey made chemistry choose a mirror image  NobelPrize.org
articles.full_text:
The Nobel prize in chemistry 2026 has been awarded to two scientists for discoveries that showed how chemical reactions can produce an overwhelming excess of one of two mirror image forms of a molecule.
Henri B Kagan at Paris-Sud University in France and Kensō Soai at Tokyo University of Science in Japan have been awarded the prize “for the discovery of nonlinear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis”.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, Sweden, on Wednesday. They will each receive an equal share of a prize of 12m Swedish kronor (about £900,000).
Many molecules, including amino acids that form the building blocks of proteins, can exist in two forms that contain the same atoms, but are mirror images of one another, much like a person’s left and right hands. This property is known as chirality.
However, the chemistry underpinning life is surprisingly “homochiral”, or same-handed. Proteins are built almost exclusively from L-amino acids, while the sugars that form the backbone of DNA and RNA have the opposite D- configuration.
How this homochirality could have emerged when chemical reactions in the laboratory typically produce equal quantities of both forms had long puzzled scientists. The question also had practical consequences: “Although these molecules look very similar, they can behave very differently when they interact with other molecules,” said Prof Andre Cobb, an organic chemist at King’s College London.
“This matters enormously for medicines because many of the molecules in our bodies, including proteins that drugs target, are themselves chiral. So the ‘left-handed’ and ‘right-handed’ versions of a drug can interact with the body in different ways which can lead to different or weakened drug effects.”
The drug thalidomide provides a potent example. During the early 1960s, thousands of children were affected by birth defects after their mothers were prescribed it to combat morning sickness during pregnancy. Researchers subsequently found differences in the biological effects of the drug’s two mirror image forms.
Manufacturers wanted a way of steering reactions towards particular forms of the molecules that they produced, and Kagan and Soai eventually provided a solution.
It began in 1986, when Kagan discovered that a relatively small imbalance between left- and right-handed forms of a catalyst could create a greater excess of one of the mirror image products than the other.
Soai took the idea further, developing a reaction in which the molecules produced themselves acted as catalysts for making more of themselves, a process known as autocatalysis. “You have to be aware, this is probably the coolest experiment in organic chemistry ever,” said Prof Peter Somfai, an organic chemist at Lund University and a member of the Nobel committee for chemistry.
In 2003, Soai demonstrated a reaction that produced almost exclusively one mirror-image form, reproducing the kind of molecular one-handedness found in living organisms for the first time.
Speaking by telephone at Wednesday’s announcement, Soai, 76, said he was “very proud” of the experiment as it offered a potential explanation for how the molecular one-handedness of life could have arisen. He described hearing the news about the prize as “one of the most exciting days of my life”.
Taken together, Kagan and Soai’s discoveries had “reshaped our understanding of molecular chirality, how it is created, amplified and transmitted”, Somfai said.
These insights have since become embedded in the development of catalysts that steer chemical reactions towards producing a particular mirror image form across different industries. “It is in the backsides of our heads all the time,” said Somfai.
“It might be difficult to say that this drug or that drug was developed using this. I would say all of them because we use this as a tool. We use this as an understanding of how to develop catalysts and how they function.”

articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Donald Trump stood inside a Maryland shipyard on October 6 and framed the war with Iran as something to be finished on a schedule. “We have to finish it up — finish it the nice way or the not-so-nice way,” he said at Anduril Industries’ Sparrows Point facility, where a $3.7 billion investment will build the largest American naval shipyard since World War II. One day earlier, Saudi Arabia had convened an emergency session in Riyadh to activate the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement for the first time — a mechanism requiring sixty days to deploy Pakistani and Turkish forces to the Kingdom. Trump’s midterm-linked timeline gives the war roughly twenty-nine days. The alliance Riyadh activated requires sixty days to reach operational readiness. Only one of those clocks belongs to someone who gets a say in when the war ends.
The risk for Saudi Arabia is not that Trump’s endgame fails. It is that it succeeds — on terms that reopen Hormuz, freeze the conflict, and remove every American incentive to address the problems the war created for the Kingdom: a $65.3 billion fiscal deficit, Houthi forces still positioned along the Red Sea coast, an untested regional defence pact, and no mutual defence treaty with the United States.
‘Finish It the Nice Way or the Not-So-Nice Way’
The Anduril event was not a war briefing. It was a domestic-industry showcase — a US Navy contract worth up to $2.9 billion, a facility Trump framed as proof that American manufacturing had returned. The war-termination language came in a press exchange, delivered between boasts about shipbuilding capacity and an observation about the difficulty of identifying who leads Iran.
“Their leaders are gone, their second group of leaders are gone, and the biggest problem I have is nobody knows who the hell is running the country,” Trump told reporters. He described the war as “essentially almost over.”
This was not the first time he anchored the timeline to the electoral calendar. On September 9, Trump said: “I think war is going to end immediately after the election because they can’t hold out any longer.” His framing has been consistent across both statements — the war ends when it becomes politically convenient, on a schedule set in Washington. The November 3 midterm is twenty-nine days away.
Vice President JD Vance reinforced the posture in a Reuters interview published the same day. “We’re not going to trade words for actions,” Vance said, demanding Iran make a “meaningful” reduction in enrichment capacity before any agreement. “If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60% enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don’t build highly enriched fuel. That’s a very basic threshold issue.”
The threshold is specific. Who negotiates it, who verifies compliance, and whether any authority in Tehran can deliver it received no mention in the interview.
What Does Victory Look Like When Nobody Knows Who Runs Iran?
Victory, as Trump describes it, requires a counterparty that can negotiate, commit, and enforce. Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed on February 28, the opening day of the US-Israeli strikes. His successor and son, Mojtaba Khamenei, has not appeared publicly since sustaining injuries in the same attack. The US intelligence community assesses the regime as “intact, but largely degraded,” with the IRGC operating as the de facto governing authority under fragmented command.
Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard told Congress that Mojtaba was “very seriously injured” and that Iranian decision-making “is not clear.” In practice, the IRGC under Major General Ahmad Vahidi has assumed the dominant role — not through constitutional succession but through the collapse of alternatives. The Soufan Center described the resulting command structure as “fragmented, decentralised.” Iran’s elected president, Masoud Pezeshkian, has said publicly that “negotiations have no meaning with an enemy that repeatedly resorts to assassination, sanctions, pressure and threats.” Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has cited the June Islamabad MOU — a framework the US effectively abandoned — as the basis for seven conditions Iran requires before reopening Hormuz.
Any agreement the US reaches with this configuration faces an enforcement problem unrelated to American military capability. The question is not whether Washington can compel a signature but whether anyone on the Iranian side commands the authority to deliver compliance across the actors who would need to comply — the IRGC’s regional commands, the Houthi leadership in Sana’a, Hezbollah’s post-war remnant. CSIS observed in its 2026 assessment that “the Trump administration has not defined what victory would look like, though it has articulated wide-reaching goals ranging from ending Iran’s nuclear program to opening the Strait of Hormuz to regime change.” Those goals require a functional counterparty. The US intelligence community’s own testimony is that no one clearly occupies that role.
Two Clocks Running Against Each Other
The MJDA activation on October 5 was presented in Riyadh as a strategic milestone. The pact’s Supreme Defence Council — convened for the first time since the agreement was signed — appointed a retired Pakistani lieutenant general as secretary general and authorised rapid deployment of Pakistani and Turkish forces to the Kingdom. Both countries committed troops. Neither has committed them to combat.
As of the activation, only Saudi forces are engaged in active operations. Pakistani and Turkish contingents occupy supportive roles. The pact’s deployment timeline — sixty days from activation to operational readiness — places full capability around early December 2026.
The readiness gap extends beyond deployment speed. The MJDA’s Supreme Defence Council directed its first-ever session on October 5; it has never directed a joint military operation. Command relationships between Saudi, Pakistani, and Turkish forces — operating under different doctrines, different rules of engagement, and different domestic political mandates — are untested under fire. Pakistan’s deployment carries parliamentary constraints. Turkey’s carries NATO coordination requirements that intersect with the same American command structure the MJDA was partially designed to supplement.
Trump’s Anduril remarks came twenty-four hours later. His September 9 statement had already linked war termination to November 3. The arithmetic is straightforward: the MJDA needs sixty days; Trump has signalled twenty-nine. If the US declares the conflict functionally over in early November — through a ceasefire, a freeze, or a drawdown timed to the midterm — the alliance Saudi Arabia activated on October 5 will not have completed deployment before the war it was built for is declared finished by the power that launched it.
The two timelines were never coordinated. Trump’s September 9 statement pre-dated the MJDA activation by twenty-six days. Riyadh activated the pact knowing the American president had already told his electorate the war would end “right after” the midterms. The sixty-day clock started anyway.
The Table Saudi Arabia Was Never Invited To
The pattern has a decade of precedent. In 2015, the P5+1 negotiations that produced the JCPOA included no Gulf Cooperation Council member at the table. Oman facilitated the secret back-channel between Washington and Tehran without informing Riyadh. Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Bahrain objected publicly — not to the existence of a nuclear deal, but to the exclusion of Iranian ballistic missiles and regional proxy networks from its terms. A decade later, those same two categories constitute the primary military threats to Saudi territory.
The deal’s architects assured Gulf capitals at the time that proxy networks and ballistic missiles would be addressed in subsequent negotiations. Those negotiations never took place. Resolution 2231, the UN Security Council’s endorsement of the JCPOA, placed limited restrictions on Iranian missile development that Iran contested and the Council did not enforce. When the Trump administration withdrew from the JCPOA in 2018, none of the categories Saudi Arabia had raised in 2015 had been addressed through any diplomatic framework.
The Abraham Accords in 2020 followed similar geometry. Saudi Arabia was widely described as the ultimate prize of the normalisation framework. The terms were drafted and signed without Saudi participation.
The Islamabad MOU of June 18, 2026, repeated the structure with sharper consequences. Pakistan mediated between the United States and Iran. The resulting framework addressed nuclear enrichment thresholds, a sequenced Hormuz reopening timeline, and ceasefire parameters. It included no provision covering Houthi operational capacity, Saudi territorial defence, or the status of missile forces positioned within range of Saudi cities and energy infrastructure. Saudi Arabia was not a signatory, not a participant, and — according to reporting by the Washington Post and the Arab Center — not consulted on the terms.
By September 2026, one diplomatic channel remained: a high-level multilateral Gulf-Iran meeting planned through Oman. Riyadh cancelled it under pressure from Houthi and Iraqi militia escalation, per the Washington Post’s September 14 report. The cancellation left Saudi Arabia in the position Foreign Policy described on September 24: MBS “called Trump twice after the East-West pipeline was hit, asking the United States to bomb the Houthis to slow their advancement, but the White House declined.”
Three times in eleven years, the United States has constructed or endorsed a framework governing Gulf security with Iran. Saudi Arabia has not co-authored any of them.
How Much Does Exclusion Cost Per Quarter?
Saudi Arabia’s Q1 2026 deficit reached $33.5 billion — SR125.7 billion — the largest quarterly shortfall since 2018. The full-year deficit has been revised to $65.

Guardian reporters Jonathan Watts and Gabrielle Canonanswered your question climate and extreme weather, from what to expect this winter in the UK to the increasing risk of natural disasters
Thank you for all your brilliant questions and for reading along! Even if yours didn’t get answered, we appreciate getting insights into what readers are interested in hearing more about as we continue our coverage – Gaby
I love Guardian readers for getting stuck into crucial topics like El Niño. Thank you for your well-informed questions. Sorry we could not answer them all – Jon
WFL5678 asks: How naive is it to hope there is some sort of climate crisis panacea to sort all this out? A game-changing discovery/invention that helps all nations/individuals be carbon negative?
Jon says: I can relate to this question, as I have found myself hoping for the same thing at certain points over the past two decades covering this beat. It was one of two useless strategies I adopted to cope psychologically with so much dismal data and depressing scenarios - the other one being the related tendency to hope I might be wrong about all of this because I am a mere journalist - and that someone much smarter than me might either prove my worst fears unfounded or come along with a smart solution.
I have since come to realise that both of these mental crutches were not just worthless but irresponsibly dangerous. Even as early as the 1980s, governments were putting off tough decisions on the climate threat on the grounds that technology and the market would find solutions. Ever since, the same excuse has been used to kick the can further down the road. We are now stuck with a whole bunch of these fake fixes, such as carbon capture and storage or blue hydrogen or carbon credits, all of which are propagated by the fossil fuel industry to extend their business models.
The latest and most damaging of these is the idea that artificial intelligence will find a solution, as long as we have enough data centres. Of course, that means using much more energy and water, which makes the fundamental problem worse. And there is no guarantee we will like the answer thrown up by a machine. What if ChatGPT or Claude or Gini or whatever AI we set up as a guru tells us the most effective climate solution is the extermination of the human race?
No, I think we should steer clear of phony or unproven remedies and stick to tried and trust solutions that climate scientists tell us will be enough - ending fossil fuels, electrifying energy, protecting ecosystems, reforesting, changing diets and reducing waste and excess consumption.
JakobLW asks: The Arabian Spring in 2011 was probably started by food shortage due to high temperatures and droughts. What are possible similar outcomes this and next year? How will El Niño affect food prices next year? Will it cause an economic disaster in 2027 or 2028?
bookishlondonlesbian asks: What kind of knock-on effects can we expect from this El Niño after it has ended?
Gaby says: There are concerns that this strong El Niño will impact agricultural bread baskets where food is grown and the supply chains that deliver around the world, driving both shortages and costs. The World Food Programme is already sounding the alarm, estimating that 274 million people in 45 countries could face food insecurity by the end of next year. Increased risk of hunger will likely impact the most vulnerable populations around the world, and the WFP is pushing for early action to mitigate the worst effects.
But a rise in extreme weather events won’t only wreak havoc on crops, livestock, and food production. It will also add challenges for factories, shipping, and transportation. Global food supply chains are already facing shocks from Donald Trump’s tariffs, the war in Iran, and strain from conditions fueled by the climate crisis. El Niño will add new layers of challenges. A rise in the number and intensity of extreme weather events can wreak havoc on crops, livestock, and food production, but also create problems for factories, shipping, and transportation. “Forecasters predict strong intensity by winter, which will likely arrive when supply chains are already stressed by tariff-driven sourcing disruptions, Strait of Hormuz shipping restrictions, and elevated fertilizer costs,” Jonathan Colehower, managing director of supply chain practice at global IT solutions firm UST said during an August interview with Reuters on the issue. Maximo Torero, chief economist at the UN Food and Agriculture Organization, has also told reporters that global food prices that are already rising because of these geopolitical pressures could climb further. Of course, the dangers posed by El Niño change region-by-region, so some places will be hit harder than others. That means, particular goods may also be affected. Coffee, chocolate, and palm oil are all produced in areas bracing for extreme weather.
What will it take for our leaders to finally see the threat from climate change?
eamonmcc asks: What will it take for elites in finance, business and politics to finally publicly admit the game is up and that climate change is the greatest threat humanity we have collectively ever faced?
Gaby says: I wish I knew the answer. It certainly feels overwhelming to see the escalating threats alongside both inaction and downright denial. One thing I can say is that while the problem is global many solutions are local. Experts have told me time and time again that we must adapt to the extremes caused by the climate crisis while we continue to push for a better future and that happens at the community level. Perhaps a silver lining of this El Niño is it may offer a glimpse of the challenges that will arise as the world warms - and there is still time to prepare.
Climate change seems to be accelerating - should we worry?
Dormant2 asks: I’m surprised how suddenly we seem to have gone from small climate effects to very noticeable ones such as this year’s heatwaves and the lateness of the first Atlantic hurricane. Is this an acceleration and is it a worry?
Jon says: This concerns me enormously. I started to be worried about this in 2023, when sea surface temperatures jolted upwards. The following year - as the trend persisted - I put a similar question to Gavin Schmidt, the director of the Nasa Goddard Institute for Space Studies in New York who said scientists were still struggling to explain whether the sudden rise was a blip or an alarming new trend.
Since then various explanations have been put forward, including the possibility that the Earth is warming faster because it is losing the heat-reflecting “albedo” effect of white snow and ice at the poles, or the widely-held view that pollution controls have reduced aerosols that previously limited the amount of sunlight reaching the earth’s surface.
Scientific opinion seems to be moving towards an acceptance of the theory that global heating has sped up over the past 15 years. Last year, Zeke Hausfather, an influential climate scientist, said there is now sufficient evidence from multiple sources - climate models, ocean heat content, and changes in earth energy imbalance - to “tips the scale toward pretty clear acceleration in recent years.”
Sometimes you can’t help wishing experts are wrong. But I trust climate scientists - who include some of the smartest people on the planet - are trying to find the truth and they are the best guides to what is happening.
funkymentalist asks: Unrelated to El Niño, what is the likelihood of the AMOC (Atlantic meridional overturning circulation) shutting down?
Jon says: I don’t think these two things are unrelated. Everything is affected by climate breakdown. And both El Niño and the slowdown of AMOC are related to the staggeringly huge amounts (see this article on zettajoules which I also referred to above) of extra energy that the oceans are being forced to absorb as a result of greenhouse gas burning.
Quick refresher for any readers who are unfamiliar with this topic: “Amoc, or the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, is a system of ocean currents that brings heat into the northern Atlantic. Warm surface water from the tropics flows north and releases its heat in the subpolar Atlantic, south of Greenland and west of Britain and Ireland. Then it cools and sinks to a depth of between 2,000m to 3,000 metres before returning south as a cold current. Amoc is one of our planet’s largest heat transport systems, moving the equivalent of 50 times the human energy use, and it has a particularly strong impact on the climate in Europe, affects the ocean’s CO2 uptake and oxygen supply, as well as rainfall patterns in the tropics.”
A collapse of AMOC would be catastrophic for large parts of the world. This was considered a remote likelihood until relatively recently. But recent studies show a much higher risk indeed. AMOC is now at its weakest for 1,600 years. One of the leading experts in the field, Stefan Rahmstorf put it to me in these terms: “It is a question of risk assessment. I compare it to being told that there is a 10% chance of an airplane crashing. Would you get on that plane? I wouldn’t. The disastrous consequences are unacceptable.”
He was speaking to me in 2024. Since then the dangers have increased. My colleague Damian Carrington wrote earlier this year of new AMOC research that “found an estimated slowdown of 42% to 58% in 2100, a level almost certain to end in collapse.”
There are many areas where climate journalists, scientists and activists feel the urge to pull their hair out in frustration at their inability to close the huge gap in understanding between the dangers we face and the action that governments need to take. For me, this is one of the worst.
Why is it called ‘El Niño’ rather than something like ‘El Monstruo Gordo’?
Rad_Mobil asks: Why is it called “El Niño” rather than something like “El Monstruo Gordo”?
Gaby says: The name “El Niño” actually harkens back to long before forecasters
