October 7 attack to Gaza ceasefire: Three years of Israel-Hamas conflict
From the October 7 attack and 251 hostages to the war in Gaza, regional escalation, ceasefires and plans for Gaza's future, here is a timeline of the key developments over three years
Listen to This Article
Three years ago, on October 7, 2023, Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups launched a terror attack on southern Israel, killing nearly 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages. What followed was a prolonged war in Gaza that expanded into a wider regional conflict, drawing in Iran-backed groups such as Hezbollah and the Houthis, while repeated ceasefire and hostage-release efforts sought to end the fighting.  
Here is a look at the key events that have shaped the conflict since October 7, 2023.
October 7, 2023: The attack
At dawn on October 7, Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups launched a surprise, multi-front assault from Gaza into southern Israel. Thousands of rockets were fired into Israel while terrorists breached the Gaza border fence. The attack killed about 1,200 people, according to the US State Department's account. Israel's later detailed accounts put the number killed at 1,192 Israelis.
Another 251 people were abducted from Israel and taken to the Gaza Strip. The hostages included Israeli civilians, including children, women, and the elderly, Israeli military personnel, and dozens of foreign nationals. The hostage issue became a defining element of the war.
Also Read
Israel declares war
Israel declared war on Hamas on October 8, 2023. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government set out three objectives: destroying Hamas' military and governing capabilities, bringing the hostages home and preventing another attack from Gaza.
The Israeli military first concentrated on regaining control of communities and military positions inside Israel and stopping further infiltration. At the same time, Israel stepped up its airstrikes across Gaza.
Gaza under bombardment
Israel's initial response escalated into a sustained campaign of airstrikes across Gaza. Israel imposed a siege and restricted the movement of goods, fuel and other supplies into the territory. By October 18, the UN reported 3,478 Palestinians killed in Gaza, with about one million people estimated to have been displaced. After weeks of bombardment, Israel expanded its ground operation into Gaza in late October 2023.
The first truce and regional spread
In November 2023, Israel and Hamas reached their first major temporary truce, mediated by Qatar, Egypt and the United States. The pause resulted in the release of scores of Israeli and foreign hostages in exchange for Palestinian prisoners and increased humanitarian aid entering Gaza. The fighting resumed after the truce ended.
The conflict also spread beyond Gaza. Hezbollah began launching rocket attacks into northern Israel from Lebanon immediately following the October 7 assault, triggering repeated Israeli strikes and exchanges of fire. In November, the Iran-backed Houthi movement in Yemen began launching drone and missile attacks against commercial shipping vessels in the Red Sea, saying they were acting in support of Palestinians. The US and other countries became involved in efforts to protect shipping.
2024: Israel targets Hamas and Hezbollah leadership
As the war continued, Israel stepped up operations targeting senior Hamas leadership. In July 2024, Israel said it had killed Mohammed Deif, the longtime head of Hamas' military wing and one of the key figures Israel associated with the October 7 attack. Hamas political chief Ismail Haniyeh was killed in Tehran in July while attending the inauguration of Iran's new president. Israel did not initially claim responsibility, but later acknowledged it.
The confrontation with Hezbollah escalated sharply in September. Thousands of pagers used by Hezbollah members exploded across Lebanon and parts of Syria, followed a day later by explosions involving the group's walkie-talkies. Hezbollah blamed Israel, which did not initially claim responsibility.
The escalation culminated in the killing of Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah in an Israeli airstrike on Beirut in September, 2024. In October, Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was killed by Israeli troops. The fighting between Israel and Hezbollah continued until Israel and Lebanon agreed to a ceasefire in November 2024.
2025: Ceasefire, renewed war and another truce
Further negotiations continued through 2024, and a new ceasefire and hostage-release agreement was reached in January 2025.
The ceasefire did not last. After negotiations broke down, Israel resumed large-scale military operations in Gaza in March 2025. In May, Israel said it had killed Mohammed Sinwar, the younger brother of Yahya Sinwar and a senior Hamas military commander.
A major breakthrough came in October 2025, when Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-backed ceasefire and hostage-release deal. The first phase took effect on October 10 and halted the large-scale Israeli military offensive while providing for the release of the remaining living Israeli hostages and Palestinian prisoners and detainees.
2026: From ceasefire to a new framework
The beginning of 2026 marked a shift towards an attempt to establish a longer-term political and security framework for Gaza. The second phase of the US-backed plan began in January, focusing on future governance, reconstruction and the disarmament of Hamas.
A Palestinian National Committee for the Administration of Gaza was announced as a transitional body, while the US-backed Board of Peace was tasked with overseeing the wider process. The last living hostage from the October 7 attack had been returned to Israel in October 2025, while the remains of the last deceased hostage, were recovered and returned in January, 2026. This completed the return of all 251 people taken captive during the October 7 attack, according to the Board of Peace's report to the UN.
The ceasefire, however, remained fragile. The UN said in February that Gaza was still not at peace, with Israeli strikes and exchanges of fire continuing despite the ceasefire.
July 2026: Hamas disarmament deal
In July, US President Donald Trump announced that the Board of Peace had reached an agreement with Hamas on the group's disarmament and the transfer of civilian and security control of Gaza to a new Palestinian technocratic government.
But the announcement did not immediately translate into implementation. Hamas said its disarmament was linked to wider political conditions, including the establishment of a Palestinian state, while Israel continued to demand the complete dismantling of Hamas' military capabilities before a full withdrawal.
September 2026: Gaza reconstruction plan
In September, the Board of Peace unveiled a $2.45 billion, six-month reconstruction blueprint covering 66 projects in infrastructure, healthcare, education, shelter and food security. But reconstruction remained dependent on progress on security and governance of the region.
Three years on
As Israel marks three years since the October 7 attack, memorial events are being held across the country, with the anniversary coinciding with preparations for a general election. The commemorations are the first since a ceasefire began in Gaza last year.
At state memorial ceremonies on Monday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said there would be no Hamas rule in Gaza and vowed to continue targeting those involved in the October 7 attack or those who held hostages.
The ceasefire has not ended the humanitarian crisis in Gaza. Hundreds of thousands of Palestinians continue to live in tents or temporary shelters, while plans for reconstruction and the territory's future governance remain uncertain. Israel says it controls more than 60 per cent of Gaza and has continued carrying out airstrikes, saying they target Hamas and those involved in the October 7 attack.

Multiple explosions rocked Kyiv in repeated waves in the early hours of Wednesday as Russia launched ballistic missiles toward the Ukrainian capital, with damage reported across several districts.
A Kyiv Post journalist in the capital reported several strong explosions after the Ukrainian Air Force warned that ballistic missiles were heading toward the city.
Several hours later, Kyiv was rocked by explosions for a second time. Ukrinform reported renewed blasts at around 5:12 a.m., shortly after the Air Force detected several more ballistic missiles heading toward the capital. The air raid alert remained in force.
The attacks came only hours after President Volodymyr Zelensky warned in his nightly address that Ukrainian intelligence had received updated information indicating Russia was preparing a “massive strike.” He urged residents to take missile alerts seriously and said Ukrainian forces were ready to respond “as much as our defenses allow.”
Ukraine’s Air Force warned of ballistic missiles heading toward Kyiv, Dnipro and Zaporizhzhia after reporting a threat from Russia’s Bryansk region and from the south.
The overnight assault also included jet-powered drones moving across several regions. The Air Force tracked such drones over northern Kyiv region, while cruise missiles were later reported over the Kharkiv and Poltava regions.
Damage reported across Kyiv
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko and the Kyiv City Military Administration reported damage in several districts as the attack unfolded.
In the Obolonskyi district, a strike was recorded in an area of non-residential development.
In Podilskyi, warehouse facilities were hit and damaged.
In Darnytskyi, burning debris fell on an open area, while in the Shevchenkivskyi district another strike hit a non-residential area.
The Kyiv City Military Administration later reported further consequences of the attack in Darnytskyi, where damage was recorded on the territory of a garage cooperative.
Air defenses were operating over the capital as officials repeatedly urged residents to remain in shelters.
Kyiv hit again before dawn
The second round of explosions came several hours after the initial ballistic missile attack.
Shortly before the renewed blasts, the Ukrainian Air Force detected several ballistic missiles heading toward Kyiv.
The repeated explosions formed part of a broader overnight Russian assault in which missiles and fast-moving drones were tracked across multiple regions of Ukraine.
The Kyiv City Military Administration reported in the morning that two people had been killed in the attack.
The State Emergency Service (DSNS) said firefighters extinguished a fire covering 200 square meters at a garage cooperative in the Darnytskyi district. The bodies of two victims were found during the firefighting operation, while two other people were rescued.
Kyiv under mounting pressure
The latest attack comes as Kyiv faces an intensifying Russian air campaign approaching winter.
Russia has increasingly targeted Ukraine’s energy and transport infrastructure, including railways, roads and bridges over the Dnipro.
The capital has also endured repeated daytime and nighttime drone attacks in recent days, while air raid sirens have sounded for prolonged periods and forced residents into shelters, basements and metro stations.
Scheduled power cuts had already plunged parts of Kyiv into darkness Tuesday evening in an effort to reduce strain on the damaged electricity grid.
Russian forces have also repeatedly struck Kyiv’s bridges in recent days, disrupting road and metro traffic across key crossings over the Dnipro.
Warning came hours before attack
Zelensky said Tuesday evening that Ukrainian intelligence had fresh information about Russian preparations for a large-scale attack.
“There is updated intelligence regarding Russia’s preparations for a massive strike,” he said, urging Ukrainians to respond to missile alerts.
He also stressed that Ukraine’s ability to repel incoming missiles remained dependent on continued weapons deliveries from allies.
The warning was followed later Tuesday by reports that three Russian Tu-160 strategic bombers had taken off from the Belaya air base.
Hours later, ballistic missiles were heading toward Kyiv and other major Ukrainian cities, followed by renewed explosions in the capital before dawn.

On October 7, 2026, Israel marks three years since the Hamas attack that killed 1,200 people and became the deadliest day in the country’s history. The attack on October 7, 2023, led to a major Israeli military operation in Gaza. Despite a ceasefire that has been in place for nearly a year, living conditions there remain critical.
As highlighted by Reuters
During the attack, militants also seized 251 hostages and took them to Gaza. More than 74,000 people have been killed in subsequent Israeli airstrikes and ground operations, according to Gaza’s health authorities.
Commemorative events are planned in Israel for the third anniversary. A memorial service is due to be held near the Gaza border at the site of the Nova music festival, where militants killed 348 young people during the attack. A separate event will take place at Hostages Square in Tel Aviv.
Anniversary comes ahead of Israeli election
This is the first anniversary with no hostages left in Gaza. Both living and deceased hostages were returned in exchanges for Palestinians held in Israeli prisons. The remains of the last Israeli hostage were returned in January.
Israel’s first election since the attack is just 20 days away. The vote is seen as a judgment on Benjamin Netanyahu’s long tenure in power.
Netanyahu has rejected responsibility for the security failure and opposed an independent inquiry. This has fueled discontent in Israel, including among the families of those killed in the attack. Some of them have joined the election race.
A survey by the Israel Democracy Institute found that, for 68% of Jewish Israelis, the events of October 7 were a very or fairly important factor in choosing a party. Polls suggest that if an election were held now, neither Netanyahu nor his main rivals would win enough seats in parliament to form a coalition.
Ceasefire has not stopped strikes in Gaza
The first anniversary of the U.S.-brokered ceasefire agreement falls on October 10. The deal halted large-scale fighting, but did not stop Israeli strikes in Gaza or lead to the disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups.
Israel initially controlled about 53% of Gaza, but Israeli forces have since expanded their control to nearly two-thirds of the territory. Hamas controls the rest. About two million people live there, most of them in temporary tents or buildings damaged by bombardment.
Donald Trump has proposed several plans for rebuilding Gaza under the so-called “Board of Peace.” They do not take into account the property rights of Palestinians whose homes were destroyed, and have won the support of neither Israel nor Hamas. Ceasefire negotiations remain deadlocked.
The sides have not agreed on the terms under which Hamas would lay down its weapons in exchange for an Israeli troop withdrawal. Israel says it will not pull back until the group is fully disarmed. Hamas has agreed to a phased process, but says it will not lay down its weapons while Israeli attacks continue.
Israel continues to bomb Gaza. According to the enclave’s health authorities, recent strikes have killed Hamas militants as well as many civilians. The casualty figures published by these authorities do not distinguish between civilians and combatants.
More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire began in October 2025, according to local health authorities. During the same period, five Israeli soldiers have been killed by militant actions or in clashes, the Israeli military says.
Three years after the attack, security, accountability for the failure and Gaza’s future remain central concerns in Israeli society ahead of the election.

The outbreak, the hostages, the assassinations: Key events that defined October 7 and the resulting war
The complete timeline of the war that changed Israel: the surprise attack, the ground offensive, the hostage release deals, the additional fronts, and the defining moments along the way
Three years ago today, the State of Israel awoke to a horrible reality, as the Hamas terrorist organization launched an unprecedented terror attack, the scale of which had never been seen before. Since then, Israel has been in one of the most complex and tumultuous periods in its history, with a war that has expanded from a single focal point to multiple regional arenas.
From the first sirens, through the ground offensives, the direct confrontation with Iran, and the hostage release deals, these are the events that have shaped the war from its beginning until today, changing Israel and the entire Middle East.
October 7, 2023 | 06:29 - The surprise attack begins
At 6:29 a.m., on Simchat Torah, Hamas launches a large-scale attack on Israel. Alongside heavy rocket barrages targeting communities in southern and central Israel, thousands of terrorists breach the border fence and infiltrate Israel by land, sea, and air.
The terrorists raid communities near the Gaza border, military posts and bases, including Be’eri, Kfar Aza, Nahal Oz, Netiv HaAsara, Nir Oz and Sderot. At the same time, they reached the Nova music festival near Re’im.
According to the Ministry of Defense, about 6,000 terrorists managed to infiltrate Israeli territory. A total of 251 people were kidnapped and brought into the Gaza Strip.
October 7 | 07:00–09:00 - The attack spreads
Simultaneously with the fighting in dozens of communities, the terrorists arrive at the Nova party. Hundreds of partygoers try to escape the scene, and many are murdered or kidnapped.
At Re'im, about 35 people fleeing the festival arrive at the kibbutz between 7:00 and 7:30 a.m. At 7:51 a.m., the first terrorists infiltrate the kibbutz; at 08:01, dozens more enter. By 9:00 a.m., about 80 terrorists are already in Re'im.
October 7 | 06:29–09:55 - The political leadership’s timeline
According to the timeline published by the Prime Minister’s Office, Netanyahu receives his first update about the attack at 6:29 a.m. At 6:44 a.m., he speaks with his military secretary and raises the issue of mobilizing reservists. At 7:30 a.m., he departs for the Kirya military headquarters, arriving sometime between approximately 8:00 and 8:22 a.m.
October 7 | Throughout the day – Battles in the Gaza border communities
The fighting continues in the communities and outposts for hours. In Be'eri, Kfar Aza, Nahal Oz, Sderot, Ofakim, Re'im, and elsewhere, residents and local security teams fight terrorists alongside police and IDF forces.
The IDF later determined that full control over all southern communities was not restored until October 10, although large-scale fighting inside most communities had already ended by October 9.
October 7 | Evening hours – Israel goes to war
As fighting continues inside Israeli territory, the air force begins extensive strikes in Gaza. At 9:23 p.m., according to IDF updates from that day, the air force strikes infrastructure used by senior Hamas figures and units. Fighting inside some communities continues beyond 10:00 p.m.
October 8, 2023 | The second front opens
A day after the Hamas attack and the raids on Gaza border communities, Hezbollah begins firing at an IDF force on the Lebanese border. Israel responds with strikes. This marks the opening of the northern front, which will remain active throughout almost the entire war and develop into a broad campaign against Hezbollah in 2024.
October 19, 2023 | The Houthis Join the Campaign
The Houthis in Yemen also enter the conflict, launching missiles and drones toward Israel. The attacks from Yemen will later develop into another front in the war, with Israeli strikes in Yemen and American operations against the Houthis.
October 27, 2023 | Israel begins the ground maneuver
After three weeks of airstrikes, the IDF significantly expands its ground operations in Gaza. Troops enter northern Gaza, and the war moves into a phase of extensive ground combat.
October 30, 2023 | The first hostage is rescued
The IDF and Shin Bet rescued in a special operation the observer Ori Megidish, who had been abducted from the Nahal Oz base. The IDF is striking a compound in Khan Yunis where, according to Israeli intelligence, Mohammed Deif — the head of Hamas's military wing, who has been at the top of Israel’s most-wanted list for years — was staying. Subsequently, Israel announced that Deif has been eliminated.

President Volodymyr Zelensky has urged Ukrainian citizens to take shelter when air raid alerts sound, citing updated intelligence reports about a massive strike planned by Moscow.
Ukrainian emergency services and the Air Force are ready to respond, Zelensky said in his evening address on Tuesday, Oct. 6, but the scale of their response depends on the air defense capabilities available to the country.
“A lot depends on our partners – every leader and every country in the world that has the defensive capabilities we need and can provide them to us,” Zelensky said, urging allies to continue supplying Kyiv as the war nears its fifth winter.
Bombers took off from Siberia
Hours later, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) reported that three Russian Tu-160 strategic bombers had taken off from Belaya airbase in Russia’s Siberian Irkutsk region.
In case the aircraft fire cruise missiles, the missiles could likely cross into Ukrainian airspace sometime after 3 a.m. local time, the Air Force said, urging citizens not to ignore air raid alerts and to stay in shelters.
Earlier warning
The evening address followed an initial warning Zelensky issued on Tuesday afternoon.
He announced the warning after a coordination meeting with government officials, military commanders and emergency services. According to the president, Kyiv was also preparing countermeasures.
At that meeting, the defense minister and the Air Force commander briefed the president on how air defense assets were being distributed and how protection was organized around key facilities.
Zelensky said the government and regional authorities had also prepared additional logistics measures in response to what he called a Russian operation against Ukraine’s logistics. Deadlines were set for many of the tasks, and the most urgent ones were already underway.
Separately on Tuesday, Zelensky chaired a meeting of the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief.
According to the president, electronic warfare systems neutralize a significant share of Russia’s Shahed drones, and the most effective approaches will be scaled up.
The meeting also set priorities for supplying Ukrainian forces with long-range drones next year, with the main goal of giving Ukraine the ability to respond in kind to Russian strikes.

Scope: This dossier assesses whether direct conflict between Russia and European NATO members represents a credible security threat or primarily a commercially driven narrative, distinguishing current confrontation, military contingency planning and industrial incentives, with separate European Union, Italian, French, German and British perspectives and an outlook to October 2031.
Executive Summary / BLUF
The evidence supports a real security risk accompanied by a substantial commercial expansion, rather than either inevitable European war or a threat manufactured solely to sell weapons.
War is already occurring in Europe through Russia’s invasion of Ukraine; direct Russia–NATO war is a separate outcome that the reviewed public record does not establish as imminent.
Denmark’s intelligence assessment of 24 September 2026 identifies a low but growing risk of limited Russian attacks, while considering an actual invasion unlikely. fe-ddis.dk
On 30 September, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte stated that there was no imminent threat to NATO territory and described the alliance as defensive. NATO Transcript
The supplied Lavrov report establishes neither an authenticated NATO decision to attack Russia nor the contents of a purported operational plan.
Commercial gains are documented: Rheinmetall reported first-half 2026 sales of €5.227 billion and an operating result of €786 million. Rheinmetall
The policy test is whether expenditure delivers usable defensive capability under accountable procurement, while preserving mechanisms that prevent a limited incident from becoming a wider war.
Europe’s Rearmament Must Buy Readiness, Not Just Revenue
Europe’s rearmament is creating financial commitments faster than it is producing evidence of usable collective defence. The contradiction matters because the Danish Defence Intelligence Service’s assessment of 24 September 2026 distinguishes a low but growing risk of limited military attacks from the conditional development of capabilities for a larger war, while the European Commission’s Readiness Roadmap 2030 schedules major improvements several years ahead. Governments must protect themselves during that interval without treating every industrial expansion as a security achievement. The governing test is whether expenditure reduces a specific vulnerability within a relevant timeframe. Otherwise, taxpayers finance commitments that constrain future budgets, manufacturers record orders before forces receive usable equipment, and diplomatic choices become tied to a procurement cycle whose commercial momentum can outlast its strategic justification.
The warning clock is conditional; public commitments are binding
The Danish Defence Intelligence Service’s September 2026 assessment retains approximate intervals of six months for a local war, two years for a regional war in the Baltic Sea region and five years for a large-scale European war. Those estimates depend on the Ukraine conflict ending or freezing, Russian conventional capabilities growing faster than Western capabilities, and Russia judging that the United States cannot or will not support European NATO countries. They describe conditional capability development, not an attack decision or a countdown beginning on publication day.
The same DDIS assessment separates those timelines from the possibility of limited attacks while the Ukraine war continues. That distinction changes the investment question: a government preparing only for a large conventional campaign could leave transport, energy networks or defence production exposed to disruption much sooner. Procurement must therefore serve different timescales without allowing the largest scenario to absorb resources needed for immediate protection.
The Commission’s Readiness Roadmap 2030 creates a second clock: initial capacity for the European Drone Defence Initiative by the end of 2026, full functionality by the end of 2027, and a functional Eastern Flank Watch by the end of 2028. These are proposed milestones, not certificates of completed protection. The interval between a threat assessment and a delivery target is where governments must demonstrate what works now, what remains vulnerable and which temporary arrangements can close the gap.
The numbers reveal a race between expenditure and absorption
France’s enacted August 2026 military programming revision sets expenditure at €57.1 billion in 2026 and €75.7 billion in 2030, excluding pensions, within a €435.7 billion envelope for 2024–2030. Germany’s 2026 provision combines €82.7 billion for the defence ministry with €25.5 billion from the special fund; its 2027 draft provides €109.7 billion and a further €30 billion respectively. The amounts establish financial scale, but they cannot establish how quickly trained personnel, maintenance capacity and operationally accepted equipment expand alongside expenditure.
The fiscal starting positions differ sharply. Eurostat’s first-quarter 2026 gross public debt ratios were 138.9% of GDP for Italy, 117.6% for France and 64.4% for Germany. These figures do not determine whether a particular defence investment is justified. They determine how costly repeated implementation failures can become: expenditure that delivers late still consumes borrowing capacity and competes with other public functions.
Industrial accounts expose another timing difference. In the first half of 2026, Rheinmetall reported €5.227 billion in sales and €786 million in operating profit, while operating free cash flow from continuing operations was negative €1.616 billion. Profitability can coexist with substantial cash absorption during expansion. The policy implication is that governments must distinguish industrial growth from delivered security, and examine whether public payments finance demonstrable progress or merely move financing pressure from suppliers to the state.
A contract can mature after the danger it is meant to address
Italy’s September 2026 DDX contract illustrates why the delivery calendar belongs at the centre of strategic assessment. Its €3.7 billion value includes €1.3 billion in options, while the two ships are scheduled for delivery in 2033 and 2035. They may serve a defensible long-term naval requirement, but neither delivery falls within the report’s outlook to October 2031. Their value cannot be counted as protection already available during that horizon.
The DDX example does not argue against long-lived platforms. It requires governments to explain the bridge between the capability they possess and the capability they are purchasing. A programme delivering in 2033 needs an explicit account of the crews, maintenance, existing equipment and supporting infrastructure that will sustain the relevant mission before delivery. Otherwise, the programme’s industrial visibility can conceal an operational interval that remains unresolved.
The Rheinmetall Unterlüss expansion shows the same transmission problem at a shorter timescale. The dossier records a €500 million investment, planned production of 140,000 artillery rounds in 2026 and 350,000 in 2027, alongside initial deliveries in the low five figures in July 2026. Factory investment, production targets and deliveries are separate measures. Only the last can begin to close an immediate equipment shortage, and delivery itself still requires acceptance, allocation and supporting arrangements.
The Commission’s Readiness Roadmap 2030 should therefore be read as a sequence of operational obligations. Its end-2028 objective for projects, contracts and financing to address priority shortfalls precedes its end-2030 target for receipt of SAFE-funded procurements. Governments must preserve that distinction in public reporting: a financed solution can remain an unresolved vulnerability until the equipment arrives and performs.
Fiscal flexibility cannot repair implementation failure
The national escape clause covering 2025–2028 allows flexibility of up to 1.5% of GDP for qualifying defence expenditure under the framework described in the dossier. That provision changes the fiscal treatment of expenditure; it does not improve the quality of requirements or accelerate a delayed production line. Treating flexibility as an expenditure target would turn a security exception into pressure to commit funds before implementation capacity is established.
Security Action for Europe, or SAFE, similarly changes access to financing without removing the need to repay loans. Italy’s €14.9 billion request received approval in February 2026. Approval establishes access under the instrument, rather than evidence of completed procurement or operational readiness. For a country whose first-quarter 2026 gross debt ratio stood at 138.9% of GDP, the distinction between available finance and effective protection has direct consequences for future budgets.
SAFE’s ceiling of 35% for components originating outside the eligible area is calculated on component costs, not simply on the headline contract value. That rule requires examination of the supply chain beneath the final platform. A procurement can satisfy an industrial objective yet remain dependent on a vulnerable input, while rapid access to an existing system can involve a different dependency. The relevant judgment must consider both the rule and the operational consequences of the chosen supplier structure.
The Commission’s end-2027 milestone of at least 40% joint procurement poses a related accounting challenge. Shared purchasing can reduce fragmentation only where requirements, interfaces and support arrangements are compatible. A favourable percentage would reveal little if the denominator were unclear or if formally joint contracts produced systems that participating forces could not sustain together.
Europe’s national contributions must work as one system

articles.full_text:
AI-powered script kiddies, once dismissed as a low-stakes nuisance, are now capable of mounting attacks that rival those of nation-state threat actors, according to Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 research team. The warning came during a briefing on early findings from the firm’s Frontier AI Defense service, launched in April 2026.
Sherrod DeGrippo, VP of Threat Intelligence at Unit 42, told the briefing that the traditional categories of cyberattack have shifted. Socially motivated groups are now being ‘enabled with the same tooling and sophistication as a state-sponsored group’ due to artificial intelligence. DeGrippo joined Palo Alto Networks to lead threat intelligence for Unit 42 in July 2026, bringing more than two decades of experience in threat intelligence.
‘This part of the landscape will continue to increase and bring in low-skilled actors that now have exponentially bigger and better capabilities than we’ve seen before,’ DeGrippo said. ‘These are people who know how to use a tool, and we’ve given them incredible tools.’
When AI Breaks the Balance Between Attack and Defence
Sam Rubin, SVP of Consulting and Threat Intelligence at Unit 42, described the situation in stark terms. There has historically been ‘a relative balance between the security and compromise of our information,’ he said, but ‘AI is breaking that balance.’
Unit 42 calls AI a ‘force multiplier’ across the entire attack chain, not just isolated stages. In its own internal tests over three weeks, the team completed the equivalent of one to two years of penetration testing, uncovering dozens of vulnerabilities across customer environments using AI pen-testing models.
Speed is a core part of the shift. Unit 42 found that AI could identify and exploit vulnerabilities, escalate privileges, and steal data all within 10 hours, a task that would normally occupy a penetration testing team for around two weeks.
The broader picture is quantified in Unit 42’s 2026 Global Incident Response Report, published February 17, 2026, based on analysis of more than 750 high-stakes incidents. The report found that AI has accelerated attack speeds by 4x over the past year. Identity-based techniques such as social engineering and credential misuse now drive 65% of initial access events, while vulnerabilities account for 22%. Separately, the report found that 90% of data breaches are linked to misconfigurations or security gaps, and that 48% of attacks involve the browser.
A real incident response case illustrates the ceiling of what AI-directed attackers can now achieve. In one case documented by Unit 42’s investigation team, a human attacker directed AI agents that used more than 50 MITRE ATT&CK techniques during a ransom attack on an enterprise network. The agent left behind an 80-page technical audit detailing dozens of exploited findings on the organisation’s security posture.
AI-Powered Script Kiddies and the Hacktivist Resurgence
The implications extend beyond organised criminal groups. Asked whether old-school hacktivism, similar to what groups like Anonymous practised, could make an AI-fuelled return, DeGrippo said it is ‘absolutely possible,’ as ‘AI is enabling individuals in ways that they have never been enabled before.’
She pointed to a newly accessible class of threat actor: people with personal grievances against former employers or businesses, who now have sufficient tooling to act on those grievances. ‘[AI] is opening up the landscape to the groups that haven’t been that much of a concern,’ DeGrippo said. ‘Individuals who have a vendetta against previous employers, a business they did business with and didn’t get what they were promised, now have the capabilities where they are well-enabled with tooling to carry out malicious activity if they want to. It’s something to watch in the landscape, and it’s probable.’
Attribution, she added, will also become harder. AI and open access to associated tools make identifying who is behind an attack, and where they operated from, increasingly difficult for defenders.
The threat of fully autonomous attacks is already concrete. JadePuffer, first documented by Sysdig’s threat research team on 1 July 2026, is believed to be the first fully agentic ransomware campaign. The operator gained initial access through CVE-2025-3248 in an internet-facing Langflow instance, then ran a destructive database-extortion playbook that autonomously retried failed steps to increase its own success rate. Security firm Expel noted that JadePuffer had significant operational gaps, including no stored decryption keys and no bitcoin address for payment, suggesting the operator was unskilled despite the AI-driven execution, an early illustration of exactly the gap DeGrippo describes.
What Organisations Can Do
Unit 42 has moved to industrialise its own AI-driven defences in response. On 22 September 2026, Palo Alto Networks announced Unit 42 Continuous Frontier AI Defense, an always-on agentic offensive security subscription powered by Anthropic’s Claude Mythos and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6-Cyber models, designed to continuously find, validate, and remediate enterprise exposures. The firm also introduced the Frontier AI Critical Defense Program on 19 August 2026, a coordinated initiative for critical infrastructure across operational technology, healthcare, commercial software, and open-source communities to deploy proactive virtual patches before attackers can exploit vulnerabilities.
DeGrippo is frank about the limits of preparation. ‘None of us are prepared for what is constantly evolving,’ she said. ‘CISOs need to think about what their agentic AI strategy is, top to bottom. They have to develop a strategy and then be willing to adapt. Organisations aren’t ready but are doing what they can to get there.’
Unit 42 recommends zero-trust architecture, stronger employee training beyond annual phishing exercises, governance of unsanctioned ‘shadow AI’ use inside organisations, and partnerships with specialist cybersecurity providers. The immediate test for any security team is whether their defences are calibrated for an attacker who never sleeps, never tires, and autonomously retries every step it fails.

Mayor of London Sadiq Khan has said the UK government is “right to call out the reprehensible actions of the Israeli government” in his statement on the third anniversary of the Hamas-led October 7 attack, sparking widespread condemnation.
After describing the attack as an “atrocity” that “we must never forget”, and vowing to “confront antisemitism wherever it rears its ugly head”, he turned his attention to Gaza.
“Today is also a moment to reflect on the unfathomable suffering and killing of Palestinians over the last three years, both in Gaza and in the West Bank,” Khan wrote.
“The UK government is right to call out the reprehensible actions of the Israeli government and apply more pressure to keep the prospect of a two-state solution alive.
“This is critical not only for upholding Palestinian human rights but for ending the cycle of terror, killing and bloodshed that has engulfed the region for decades and destroyed countless lives, Israeli and Palestinian alike.
“Today – more than ever – I pray that Israelis and Palestinians can one day live side-by-side in two states and in peace, with dignity, security and prosperity for both peoples.”
Reacting to Khan’s message, the Israeli embassy told the JC: “It is completely inappropriate for the Mayor of London to have tainted his statement today by pivoting to attacking the state of Israel.
“Hate marches will be taking place today on his streets and we await his condemnation of them.
“Today Jewish Londoners are marking the anniversary of the worst massacre of Jews since the Holocaust. It is a day for mourning, remembrance, and solidarity with a community that has lived with fear and a surge in hatred ever since.
“The Mayor of London chose to use this moment to turn to the ‘unfathomable suffering and killing of Palestinians’, and to criticise what he calls the ‘reprehensible actions’ of the Israeli government. Whatever one's views on the war, the timing is callous. Remembrance of the victims of October 7 should not be treated as an occasion for political positioning.”
Laila Cunningham, the Reform UK candidate for Mayor of London in 2028, said: “October 7 is not the day for Sadiq Khan to lecture Israel. It is the anniversary of the day 1,200 people were slaughtered by Hamas terrorists, and hundreds were dragged into captivity.
“Jewish Londoners are already being forced to endure a pro-Palestinian march through their city on the anniversary of the worst massacre of Jews since the Holocaust.
“The very least they deserved from their Mayor today was unequivocal solidarity.
“Instead, even on October 7, Sadiq Khan couldn’t give them that.”
Alex Hear, Chair of Labour Against Antisemitism, also addressed the mayor’s comments, saying: “A mayor who represents all Londoners should understand that on this day, above all, the Jewish community needed to be heard and comforted, not told where its grief fits among other priorities.”
Gavin Stollar OBE, chair of Liberal Democrat Friends of Israel, added: “Today the world remembers the 1,200 men, women and children murdered by Hamas terrorists, and the hundreds more injured and those taken hostage and tortured.
“There are 364 other days for the Mayor to opine on what has happened since - not today.”

Large fires have broken out at a major oil pipeline and storage facility in Russia’s Samara Oblast, according to footage shared on social media and NASA satellite monitoring.
Footage posted to social media showed large fires and clouds of black smoke above the facility, which is a major node in Russia's network of oil pipelines.
NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), which uses satellite data to detect thermal anomalies and fires, detected multiple hotspots at the facility.
The facility, which is located near the village of Prosvet, in Samara Oblast, includes pumping stations, tank farms, and blending stations. It has been a repeated target during Ukraine's campaign of deep strikes against Russian oil infrastructure.
Earlier that day, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky alluded to a Ukrainian strike on oil facilities in Samara Oblast, without specifying which facility had been hit.
While the cause of the current fire has yet to be officially stated, earlier on Oct. 7 Ukraine's General Staff confirmed damage caused to the facility in a previous Ukrainian drone strike on Oct. 2.
"As a result of the October 2, 2026 strike on the LVDS "Samara" in Prosveta, Samara Oblast of the Russian Federation, damage to eleven RVS-20000 tanks, three RVS-50000 tanks, sections of pipelines, and an automated oil production station was confirmed," the General Staff said in a statement.
The strikes on Russian oil infrastructure are aimed at "reducing the military-economic potential of the Russian Federation," they said.

A Palestinian has been killed and 16 others wounded in a pogrom by settlers under the protection of Israeli forces in the northern occupied West Bank, Palestinian authorities said.
Ali Hassan Yasser al-Bazzari, 44, from Burqa, northwest of Nablus, was killed in the attack on Palestinians harvesting olives on farmland near Burqa, west of Nablus, the Palestinian Ministry of Health said on Wednesday.
Several of those wounded, including a woman, were taken to hospitals in Tulkarem and Nablus, the Palestinian Wafa news agency reported, citing local sources.
The Palestine Red Crescent Society (PRCS) said its teams treated five people in the area, including two who suffered gunshot wounds, while the other three were beaten, Wafa reported.
PRCS said Israeli forces also assaulted ambulance crews trying to reach the injured people, and briefly detained three paramedics and a volunteer.
The Palestinian Foreign Ministry condemned the attacks, describing them as “war crimes”.
In a statement, the ministry urged the international community to fulfill its “legal and moral responsibilities” and provide international protection for Palestinians.
Al Jazeera’s Nida Ibrahim, reporting from Ramallah, said the violence comes amid escalating attacks on Palestinians during the olive harvest season.
“If you just go to pick your olives now … you could not return from the journey. It could be dangerous, not only because of Israeli restrictions against farmers going to their lands, but also because of the armed Israeli settlers who continue to assault Palestinians,” Ibrahim said.
She said the attacks have transformed an important social and economic season for Palestinian families.
“In October, usually Palestinians take days off from their jobs and go to the land, try and pick their olives because this is supposed to be a joyous season,” she added.
Israeli forces and settlers also assaulted several Palestinians harvesting olives near Anata in the central occupied West Bank, Wafa reported.
Elsewhere, settlers cut down at least 50 olive trees belonging to the Palestinian Siam family after attacking the village of Mikhmas, northeast of occupied East Jerusalem.
Ibrahim said attacks have affected olive farming, with at least 45,000 trees destroyed across the occupied West Bank this year.
Settler violence, backed by army raids
Since October 7, 2023 there have been almost 15,000 settler attacks in the occupied West Bank, with 66 Palestinians killed, according to the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission.
One such pogrom, backed by Israeli forces in the village of Marda, north of Salfit, injured a number of Palestinians picking olives on Wednesday. They were treated for tear gas inhalation by the PRCS, according to Wafa, which says Israeli forces detained at least three Palestinians.
Separately, a Palestinian was injured after being shot with live ammunition by Israeli forces during a raid near the al-Aqsa restaurant in Jenin. The injured man was taken to hospital by PRCS.
Israeli forces detained a Palestinian and imposed a curfew on residents in Burqa, as settlers raided the village east of Ramallah.

articles.title: At least 20 killed as Russia launches ‘massive’ attack on Ukraine - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: At least 20 killed as Russia launches ‘massive’ attack on Ukraine  Al JazeeraChildren killed while they slept as Russian missile kills 19 in block of flats  BBCUkraine war briefing: Zelenskyy condemns ‘vile’ attacks from Russia that killed 20 in one apartment  The GuardianDeadly Russian strikes cut power in several Kyiv districts  Financial TimesRussia hits Ukraine with wave of attacks on Putin’s birthday  POLITICO.eu

At least 20 people, including children, have been killed as Russia launched a barrage of drones and missiles across Ukraine, according to Ukrainian authorities.
Ukraine’s air force said on Wednesday that Russia launched 130 drones, 48 cruise missiles, and an unspecified number of ballistic missiles in the overnight attack. It added air defence units downed 161 targets.
Ukraine’s capital, Kyiv, and Poltava in central Ukraine, the southeastern region of Dnipropetrovsk, and Kharkiv in the northeast were the focus of the Russian attacks, authorities said.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a social media post that Russia had fired 70 missiles and also drones in one of its biggest attacks since Moscow launched the war in 2022.
“One of the key targets was our energy infrastructure. The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively,” Zelenskyy said.
The attacks also damaged residential buildings, industrial facilities, and infrastructure, according to Ukrainian officials.
In Pryluki, in the northern Chernihiv region, a Russian missile slammed into a five-storey residential building, regional authorities said. At least 14 people, including four children, were killed and 50 others wounded, emergency services said.
Kyiv’s Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people were killed in the densely populated Darnytskyi neighbourhood in a fire caused by an air attack.
Two people were killed when missiles hit high-rise buildings in Dnipro and Kremenchuk in central Ukraine, while two others died in Oleksandriya, Zelenskyy said.
‘Massive’ attack
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said its forces carried out a “massive strike” on military-industrial facilities in Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions, using high-precision land-, sea-, and air-launched weapons, as well as drones.
Targets included sites where the company Fire Point makes and stores Flamingo cruise missiles and medium- and long-range drones in Kyiv, as well as in the regions of Kyiv, Chernihiv, Kirovohrad, Dnipropetrovsk, Poltava, and Kharkiv, it said.
The attacks also targeted port and ship-repair infrastructure in the Odesa region, as well as vessels it said were being used in the interests of Ukraine’s armed forces, the ministry added.
“Ukraine has once again been hit by Russian missiles throughout the night,” Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s parliamentary commissioner for human rights, said on Telegram.
“Another sleepless night, another act of terror, after which people still have to plan their working day despite everything,” he added.
Kyiv has come under relentless bombardment in recent weeks, with Russian air attacks on energy infrastructure, rail and road transport, including the bridges that connect the city over the Dnipro River.
Air raid sirens have sounded almost constantly, urging residents to take cover in basements, shelters and subway stations.
In a separate post, Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces hit four Russian targets over the last 24 hours, including two oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara, and Astrakhan regions, as well as carrying out a response in the Black Sea.
He called the attacks a “just” response to Moscow’s strikes, and added that the facilities hit helped “Russia finance and wage its brutal war”.
Concerns over Black Sea navigation
As the war intensifies and expands, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has pressed Russian President Putin to ensure safe navigation in the Black Sea.
A statement by the Turkish presidency said Erdogan reiterated his offer to help facilitate direct talks between Russia and Ukraine, saying that safe Black Sea access was important to Ankara.
The conversation between the Turkish and Russian leaders came after drones hit two commercial vessels early on Tuesday as attacks on Black Sea shipping increase amid an intensifying Russia-Ukraine war. One vessel caught fire, while the other sank.
Bulgarian authorities say they have ended search operations after confirming that no survivors were found from the ship that sank off the country’s coast.

articles.title: Ukraine’s secret operation is making Russia nervous – and reversing Putin’s gains - The i Paper
articles.summary: Ukraine’s secret operation is making Russia nervous – and reversing Putin’s gains  The i PaperUkraine Claws Back Land in the Donbas, Thwarting a Russian Push  The New York TimesThe War Room newsletter: Operation Vivaldi is wrong-footing Russia  The EconomistSilence, Delusion and Robots: Ukraine’s Eastern Advances  Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA)Ukraine’s surprise robot offensive exposes a vulnerability in Putin’s war machine  CNBC
articles.full_text:
On an unremarkable day in May, in near-total secrecy, Ukraine quietly launched one of its most audacious fightbacks against Russia to date.
The first rumours came over summer. A few analysts and military bloggers noticed more movement than usual at a crucial point near Lyman, a city in Ukraine’s Donetsk region. Ukrainian forces seemed to be counter-attacking there, where over the past year, Russia had been making slow but steady gains.
Ukraine played it down as “limited in scope” and battlefield trackers logged little change in territory. But by the start of September, Russian milbloggers were nervous, describing a difficult situation on the front.
“It seems to me that the Ukrainians have been conducting a counteroffensive for 2.5 months, which our command is trying not to notice,” Anatoly Radov, a prominent pro-war commentator, said on 6 September.
It was only on 15 September that Ukraine finally acknowledged something large-scale had been taking place. Andrii Biletskyi, commander of the 3rd Army Corps, announced that Ukrainian forces – under maximum operational secrecy – had been conducting a groundbreaking offensive called “Operation Vivaldi”.
“A devastating blow has been dealt to the combat effectiveness of the Russian 20th and 25th Armies,” Biletskyi said.
For months, Moscow had been pushing to encircle Ukraine’s fortress belt cities, including major targets Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, and in January its troops were at the outskirts of Lyman, a crucial logistics, road and rail hub. Its capture would have handed Moscow a staging base for an offensive against Sloviansk. Vivaldi has blunted the northern claw of that pincer movement.
“Vivaldi is critical for Ukraine’s war effort overall,” Mykola Bielieskov, a research fellow at the National Institute for Strategic Studies think-tank in Kyiv, told The i Paper.
The near-total secrecy of the offensive, not to mention its tactics and use of robot technology, have reversed months of Russian gains, despite Ukrainian manpower disadvantages and the difficulties posed by the drone-dense kill zone.
The Russian delusion factor
Under a media blackout, Ukraine has seized 147 square kilometres of territory during Operation Vivaldi, according to the Washington-based Institute for the Study of War (ISW).
Ukraine’s real-time gains could be even higher. The announced advances are likely months-old and details are still being carefully controlled by Ukrainian officials. The ISW has said its own mapping methodology is “likely underestimating the extent of Ukrainian gains”.
It added that since March, Russia’s rate of seizing territory from Ukraine has been significantly declining – or even negative.
Ukraine’s information blackout appears to have played a major part in its success. “Often offensives are given away before they start, giving Russia time to move units around and get into a position to counter the advance. So, secrecy in the lead-up is really important,” said Sam Cranny-Evans, an associate fellow in military science at the Royal United Services Institute. “In some cases, it has taken the Russians a while to realise that they were under attack or the scale of the advance.”
Biletskyi warned those watching events unfold not to share “spoilers” that could imperil the ongoing operation. “Vivaldi, as is well known, has four seasons,” he warned, in reference to the Italian composer’s famous violin concerti. Biletskyi announced the completion of Operation Vivaldi’s second and third “seasons” towards the end of September.
“Operational security is enormously important in warfare,” Scott Boston, a senior defence analyst at the Rand Corporation, told The i Paper. “The Russians in particular have a lot of reconnaissance capabilities, including drones, and the more they are fixated on Kostyantynivka or Kramatorsk or Dobropillia, the less they might be noticing and responding elsewhere where there’s a successful operation going on.”
Bielieskov has claimed that maskirovka – a Soviet military doctrine of deception – helped Ukraine take advantage of poor communication within the Russian military.
“Russia has repeatedly shown an unwillingness to report bad news up the chain of command,” said Boston. “When that happens at multiple levels it really dilutes the effect of their potential advantages.”
The extent of that culture was demonstrated last month when Vladimir Putin claimed that Russia had captured the city of Svyatohirs’k, west of Lyman and far behind Ukrainian lines. Shortly afterwards, Biletskyi posted a video of himself in central Svyatohirs’k.
“I want to address the Russian military and military political leadership. Take off your clown noses and colourful wigs. Stop making fools of yourselves,” he said.
Russian military bloggers have shown their frustration over Moscow’s detachment from the reality on the ground. Radov published a recording – now deleted – which he said he sent to a Russian officer, asking: “Is there a guy among you – for f**k’s sake – who can tell Uncle Vova [Putin] that his picture isn’t actually all that pretty… we’re totally f**ked on the Lyman front.”
Tactics and technology are changing the game
During Operation Vivaldi, Ukraine has deployed innovative battlefield tactics, including novel uses of bomber drones, kamikaze robots and electronic warfare (EW). Robert G Rose, chief research officer at the Modern War Institute at West Point, the US military academy, said: “The Ukrainian corps performed this masterpiece by achieving drone dominance over Russian forces.”
Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps said EW units had disrupted more than 20,000 Russian drone missions by detecting, jamming and suppressing their signals to conceal Ukrainian attacks.
“For a long time, Ukraine has been building up its EW capabilities, devolving them to the lowest echelons possible and connecting them to other systems as much as possible,” said Cranny-Evans.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces have saturated Russian rear areas, using drones like the AI-enabled Hornet to enable 30-200-kilometre strikes against logistics, command posts, drone control centres and river crossings.
Ukraine has also sent in heavy bomber drones to air-drop ground robots equipped with grenade launchers miles behind Russian lines, and claims to have filled two Soviet-era armoured personnel carriers with explosives, converting them into giant robotic systems to slam into Russian positions.
“They have changed the game by developing a whole new approach that focuses on their relative strengths in robotics systems,” said Boston.
According to Bielieskov, Vivaldi has “proved that the same technology that led to stalemate in 2023-25” is useful for bringing more movement to the battlefield. “The trick is quality of training and leadership of officers,” he said.
What Vivaldi means for the war
Ukraine claims Russian losses, both dead and injured, across the three announced seasons have so far totaled 5,000, with hundreds taken prisoner. However, the latest offensive is unlikely to change the course of the war.
“In terms of the entire size of the occupied territories in Ukraine, it is fair to say this is a relatively small area,” Boston said. “However, given the circumstances and the overall Russian advantage in men and materiel, it is impressive.”
By reversing months of Russian gains, Vivaldi also represents a setback for Putin’s war aims of seizing the Donbas.
“Oleksandrivka, Vivaldi and various others have successfully pushed Russian units back and frustrated some of their goals for the year,” said Cranny-Evans. However, he said it was important to balance this out. “Whilst it is good and encouraging to see Ukraine advancing, the Russians are still advancing in some areas, and their strikes against Ukraine’s power infrastructure and even its data centres are really taking a toll.”
Rose added that to alter the course of the war, “Ukraine will have to envision Vivaldi on a grander scale… only such a decisive Ukrainian battlefield victory will force Russian President Vladimir Putin, Russian elites and the common Russian soldier to reappraise the war”.
Even so, as the Vivaldi offensive moves into its fourth season, Biletskyi warned that the “music continues”.

Jimmy Kimmel wasted no time condemning President Donald Trump over his viral remarks about Iran destroying American cities.
At a rally in Nebraska on Monday, Trump discussed rising prices tied to the ongoing Iran war, calling them “a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe.”
“They could take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles; let them take out San Diego,” he said next, drawing cheers from the crowd. “This is a very small price to pay. And it’s gonna be over with very soon.”
Kimmel played the clip of Trump’s speech on his show Tuesday, drawing boos from his live studio audience (which is based in Los Angeles).
“You’re booing, but they’re cheering!” Kimmel noted of Trump’s Republican crowd.
“I know he says a lot of crazy things. I know this is something we’ll forget about by Thursday when he accidentally swallows a baby at a rally or whatever the hell he does next. But that’s one of the craziest, indefensible statements I’ve ever heard even this maniac make,” the host continued.
“Openly musing about Iran, a country we are currently at war with, taking out two taking out two American cities while his adoring fans cheer him on. But it’s okay because we’re liberals. We deserve to get bombed.”
He continued: “Can somebody please change this man’s diaper already? I think that old nut has been sitting in his own excrement too long. He has the rant-a virus and it needs to be treated medically. Now we have our own president wishing death to America.
“We already had a huge bomb here this weekend. It’s called Digger,” Kimmel added in a jab at Tom Cruise’s box office bomb.
“This is insane,” Kimmel went on. “It really is. Even from him. And do you remember how upset the red hat club was when I did a joke about Trump and Melania’s May-December romance?” Kimmel was referring to a joke in which he described Melania as having “the glow of an expectant widow,” a gag he later claimed was about the 24-year age gap between the president and first lady.
The joke drew backlash from conservative commentators, several of whom branded Kimmel’s remarks “dangerous.” He then played a series of clips from conservative media figures criticizing him.
“If that rhetoric was deranged and dangerous and violent and dark, surely you must be mortified by the president of the United States casually ruminating about the deaths of 13 million people,” Kimmel said, before cutting to conservative commentator’s defending the president’s remarks.
One news commentator is shown saying: “The question on everyone’s mind is: Why can’t the left take a joke?”
“That’s right,” Kimmel replied. “You know what? I’m going to report him to the FCC. The hypocrisy is so glaring you can’t even turn your head toward it. You will get blinded. Do you want to know the real reason Trump hates California? I’ll tell you. It has nothing to do with politics.”
He then showed a clip of California Governor Gavin Newsom greeting Melania with a kiss.
“It’s because our governor got farther with his wife than he has in 15 years,” Kimmel added. “And she’s been California dreaming ever since.”
The White House has since blasted media coverage of Trump’s remarks about Iran “taking out” U.S. cities, arguing that news outlets had taken his comments out of context.
On X, White House Communications Director Steven Cheung wrote: “The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality. He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped. America is safer because of the President.”

articles.summary: ‘There will be no Tel Aviv’: Egyptians threaten Israel following Smotrich Sinai comments  The Jerusalem PostEgypt rejects dragging Sinai’s name into Israeli Finance Minister’s statements, source says  Egypt TodayEgyptian TV host Ahmed Moussa issues harsh message against Israel  Egypt IndependentIsraeli minister Smotrich threatens Egypt ahead of 1973 October war anniversary  The New ArabSmotrich Threatens to Occupy Sinai and Angry Reactions in Eg &nbsp...

Egyptian media channels widely aired threats against Israel, Tel Aviv, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu this week as they reacted angrily to Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s warning Monday that Israel would destroy Sinai if Egypt attacked Israel, delivered during an interview with the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) news site Hashtiblach.
“What will cause Egypt not to attack us? They know that if they attack, there will be no Sinai,” Smotrich told the channel. “It won’t happen again. There is no [Menachem] Begin.”
Then-prime minister Menachem Begin made peace with Egypt by signing the historic Egypt-Israel Peace Treaty on March 26, 1979. Under the treaty, Israel agreed to withdraw its forces and civilians from the Sinai Peninsula in phases, while Egypt regained full sovereignty over the territory, and the two countries established security arrangements governing their forces in the peninsula.
“At least half of Gaza under tomorrow morning, and the same thing with Lebanon, up to 8, 9, [or] 12 kilometers that are ours. Guys, it won’t be [yours], you’re not coming back. Why? Because you started with us, and that’s the price of war,” Smotrich said.
Though his threat made clear that such an action would only be taken if Egypt attacked Israel, in the wider context of Israel’s post-October 7 security, his words were poorly received in Egypt. Egyptian parliamentarian and journalist Mustafa Bakri described the minister as an “extremist Zionist… thug” and insisted that Cairo could “crush” Israel’s military.
“[Smotrich] thinks Egypt is an open playground. I wish you would read how we crushed your army, you ignorant fool – the ones who did it once are capable of repeating it again.
“The Egyptian army is ready to confront and crush anyone whose soul dares to tamper with national security,” Bakri wrote. “You will surely be taken prisoner, and we’ll throw you in the mental hospital in Khanka. Don’t you dare overstep again, you madman [he said, addressing Smotrich].”
Egyptian TV host: Israel would pay 'heavy price' if it attacked
Egyptian TV host Ahmed Moussa, on Ala Mas’ouleety [Egyptian nightly talk show broadcast on the satellite channel Sada El Balad], also commented on Smotrich’s remarks, responding by insisting that “all 120 million Egyptians would die defending Egypt, and Israel would pay a heavy price if it took any step threatening Egyptian national security.”
Moussa noted Egypt’s success in the Yom Kippur War, during which more than 200 Israeli soldiers were taken prisoner by Egyptian forces, saying that this time there would be no hostages to exchange.
“If you act recklessly, there will be no Israel. You cannot get near an inch of Sinai, and what happened in 1967 will not be repeated with Egypt.”
“We are advocates of peace, but some extremists in the Zionist entity do not want peace. Egypt is a strong country. The war criminal says he will take Sinai. This is harassment and a threat to Egypt. We know what the lesson of 1973 was like for you,” Moussa said.
“You are an illegitimate state. We brought you back with the prisoner exchange, and after that there will be no prisoner exchange because there will be no prisoners.”
'There will be no Tel Aviv, there will be no Ben-Gurion Airport'
Amr Adib, on MBC Egypt, insisted that Cairo had actively worked to defend the border with Israel from any instability, and if the IDF attacked, “There will be no Tel Aviv, there will be no Ben-Gurion Airport, and there will be no Netanyahu.”
“Before you decide to finish us, you will be finished,” he said. “Before you throw us into the sea, you will be in the sewer.”
Egyptian political science professor Hamed Fares told Sky News Arabia that Smotrich’s comments reflected a form of “political adolescence” and demonstrated, in his view, the minister’s ignorance of the region’s power dynamics.
Fares added that he believed Smotrich’s comments, which he described as a “redline” for Egypt, reflected the finance minister’s efforts to maintain a hardline image ahead of the upcoming elections.
Fares said that by portraying neighboring countries as unstable, Smotrich was seeking to create a perceived need for territorial expansion on national security grounds.

articles.title: Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai win Nobel Prize in chemistry - NPR
articles.summary: Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai win Nobel Prize in chemistry  NPRNobel Prize in Chemistry Is Awarded to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai  The New York TimesExplainer: what are autocatalysis and non-linear effects and why have they won the 2026 Nobel prize in chemistry?  Chemistry WorldA Nobel for illuminating life’s asymmetry  The EconomistThis Rice University professor has helped pick more than a dozen Nobel Prize winners  Houston Public Media

Scientists win chemistry Nobel for discoveries about mirrored molecules that led to many drugs
STOCKHOLM — Scientists Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in chemistry Wednesday for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs and transformed modern medicine.
Many molecules come in versions that look alike but are not exactly identical, like right and left hands. Kagan, who is from France, and Soai, from Japan, found ways to make chemistry pick a side, describing and designing reactions to produce the desired mirror image.
"The medicines we have today would not be possible without this chemistry," said Rigoberto Hernandez, president of the American Chemical Society.
Soai was shopping at a neighborhood supermarket when he heard he had won.
"I'm very excited to receive the very nice news," Soai told the Nobel committee and journalists by phone. "Of course, this is one of the most exciting days in my life."
The discovery enabled most modern medicines
Mirror images of the same molecule can have different properties. For example, one version of the chemical carvone smells like mint, while the other has a whiff of caraway, a spice often used in rye bread.
The alternate versions can also behave differently when interacting with other chemicals. When designing drugs to treat diseases, scientists are choosy about which mirror image they use. They want the version of a molecule to treat a cold, not one that will make the sniffles worse.
In the 1980s, Kagan's work showed there might be a way to design reactions to produce one form of a molecule over the other. Years later, Soai perfected the process. He created the first-ever chemical reaction to efficiently produce only one of a molecule's mirror images, in what's now known as the Soai reaction.
"This is probably the coolest experiment in organic chemistry," said Peter Somfai, a member of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry.
Kagan, 95, is affiliated with the Université Paris-Sud in Orsay, France. Soai, 76, is affiliated with the Tokyo University of Science. The Nobel committee described their work as a feat never previously achieved by anyone "other than life itself."
The French Academy of Sciences, where Kagan is a member, congratulated him, as did French President Emmanuel Macron, who called the prize "an immense source of pride for the country" and "a recognition befitting a lifetime of research."
"It might be difficult to say that this drug, or that drug, was developed using this," Somfai said. "I would say all of them, because we use this as a tool, we use this as an understanding, how to develop catalysts, how they function."
Life, too, prefers one mirror image over the other. DNA twists to the right, and the proteins in human bodies are made of mostly left-handed building blocks.
In addition to developing better medicines or perfumes, deciphering the mirror images of molecules can help scientists understand the chemical architecture of life, said chemist Holden Thorp, editor-in-chief of the journal Science.
"There are still fascinating aspects that remain unknown and surely more yet to be discovered," Soai said at a news conference hosted by his university in Tokyo. "I hope to do what I can, however modestly, to contribute to help advance research in this field."
Japan's largest newspaper, Yomiuri, distributed an extra edition with a headline proclaiming "Nobel Prize Mr. Soai," with a big photo of the scientist. The papers quickly disappeared as office workers picked them up on their way home.
More Nobel prizes are still to be awarded
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winner in Stockholm.
Last year, three scientists won the chemistry Nobel for their development of new molecular structures that can trap vast quantities of gas inside, laying the groundwork to potentially suck greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere or harvest moisture from desert environments.
This year's prizes began with the Nobel for medicine, awarded Monday to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award announced Tuesday recognized a scientist's efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos.
The literature prize is set to be awarded Thursday. After Friday's peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, a small group of laureates or an organization.
Correction Oct. 8, 2026
