articles.title: His pregnant wife was murdered in front of him on Oct. 7. Three years later, he still talks to her - Ynetnews
articles.summary: His pregnant wife was murdered in front of him on Oct. 7. Three years later, he still talks to her  Ynetnews‘Neither war nor peace’: Palestinians in Gaza on existing amid disease, despair and ruins  The GuardianHow Israeli and Palestinian kids are coping 3 years after the Oct. 7 Hamas attacks ignited the Middle East  CBS NewsOpinion | 3 years after Oct. 7, the world's reaction to Gaza exposes a painful truth  MS NOWLife In Gaza, Three Years After October 7...
articles.full_text:
Three years have passed since that Saturday, but for Hamid Abu Arar, the day never ended.
“Every day I live October 7, 2023,” he says. “You can’t ignore it or forget it. You have nine children at home who lost their mother, and they remind you of October 7 every day, every hour, every minute. They ask for their mother, ask why she isn’t coming back. I thought that as they grew older, they would understand, that maybe slowly it would leave their minds. But exactly the opposite happened.”
That morning, Abu Arar was driving to his agricultural job with his pregnant wife, Fatma, and their son Elias when Hamas terrorists who had invaded Israel opened fire on them. Fatma, who was four months pregnant, was murdered before his eyes. Hamid and Elias, then about six months old, were wounded.
Hamid hid with the baby for hours, listening as the terrorists spoke Arabic among themselves and discussed plans to attack civilians and Israeli security forces.
“I was in a state I had never experienced in my life,” he recalls. “I’m wounded in my shoulder and leg, my baby is wounded, my wife was murdered in front of me, and I don’t know where I am. The terrorists didn’t leave the area for a moment. They went to different places and came back to the junction, and I could hear them clearly. I heard their plans.”
At one point, he says, the terrorists prepared an ambush for an approaching IDF force. Hamid’s phone had already died after he spent hours passing information to Israeli security forces.
“I heard Hebrew from the other direction. I looked and saw the army,” he says. “The first thing that went through my head was: That’s it, our chance of surviving is over. They’ll start shooting at each other and we’re in the middle.”
“Then I told myself, ‘Hamid, you’re a strong man. You need to make a quick decision. You have to save the situation.’”
He removed his shirt, fearing that the soldiers might mistake him for a terrorist or believe he had kidnapped the baby, and walked toward them.
One soldier opened fire. “The bullets passed by my head, and some of the shrapnel went into my back. I was hit by 11 fragments. The officer shouted, ‘Cease fire, Israeli, Israeli.’”
Hamid continued toward the soldiers and warned them about the ambush. “The terrorists were waiting for them,” he says. “One wanted to open fire at the soldiers, and the other told him to wait, to let them come another seven or eight meters closer. They wanted to hit them at point-blank range. The soldiers were advancing without knowing. It was certain death.”
‘Mom blood, Mom blood’
After the soldiers fought the terrorists, Hamid and Elias were evacuated to Soroka Medical Center. But for Hamid, that was when the real battle began. Hamid and Fatma’s nine children, seven girls and two boys, were all young when they lost their mother. Their oldest is now only 11.
Elias is now 3, and his father says he is receiving treatment from an early-childhood psychiatrist for trauma. When Elias was around 2, Hamid began noticing changes.
“The child became angry, aggressive. At night you could see his hand shaking,” he says. “I took him for treatment and they told me he was experiencing trauma. I said to the doctor, ‘But he was six months old. What does he understand? What does he remember?’”
Then came a moment that changed Hamid’s own understanding. “Two or three months ago, Elias came to me while I was sitting in the living room and said, ‘Dad, I have a big gun.’ I asked him who he wanted to shoot. He couldn’t explain and said, ‘Mom blood, Mom blood.’ Like he meant the person who killed his mother.”
Hamid immediately got up, hugged him and told him his mother was in heaven. He then bathed him, changed his clothes, took him out to buy something and drove with him to the cemetery.
“He and I washed his mother’s grave,” Hamid says. “He calmed down. We went home and he slept.” It is only one moment, he says, in the daily reality of their home. “There is hardly a day without some crisis. If it isn’t this child, it’s that daughter. Every day, another one remembers Mom. Listen, I’m living a life that only Allah knows how I survive and how I cope with the children. There are nine of them. All I can say is that there is Allah in heaven.”
When Hamid speaks about Fatma, he is not talking only about the woman he lost, but about the life they almost had together. His voice breaks and he struggles to hold back tears. “We were a special couple. We met, we loved each other and built our life hand in hand. She was my right hand.”
‘Hamas destroyed everything’
Fatma was a beautician, and the couple had planned to open businesses of their own. They had already found a location in Rahat for her salon, which she planned to open with a partner.
“On the evening of October 7, I was supposed to sign the contract for her shop,” Hamid says. “We had already found the place, and then the Hamas terrorists came and destroyed everything. They left us no dream, nothing.”
The one dream that remains, he says, is the one they shared for their children: education. “Today I take care of the children. I even pay for private teachers for them and strengthen them,” he says. “I have very smart children. I promised them, and I am continuing Fatma’s dream.”
Hamid has not returned to work since October 7. His life revolves entirely around his nine children: driving them, picking them up, arranging schools, treatment and studies.
But he also needs treatment himself. “I live on five kinds of pills,” he says. “What can I do? Otherwise I can’t cope.”
Even with treatment, he cannot stay away from the place where his previous life ended. “There isn’t a week or 10 days that goes by without me going to the Gaza border area. I have to. I feel like I live there. My wife is there. My soul is there.”
He drives to the junction, sits there and sometimes stays for hours. “I just sit, smoke, talk to Fatma. I’m always telling her about the children.”
Elias, he says, looks exactly like Fatma. Perhaps that is also one reason the bond between father and son has become nearly inseparable. “If I go to Be’er Sheva to run errands, I do everything like a missile, fast, fast, so I can get back to Elias,” he says. “I can’t be without him. He is the air I breathe.”
Abu Arar’s story is also shaped by the identities that collided that morning. He was born in Gaza, grew up in Rafah and is a Muslim from a religious family. His Muslim wife was murdered by Hamas terrorists.
“What happened on October 7 has nothing to do with religion, unequivocally,” he says. “I know the Quran very well. To come to innocent people while they are sleeping, to babies, children and women and murder them in cold blood, where is that written? Our Islam is completely different.”
He says the terrorist who shot Fatma knew she was Arab. “He saw a religious Muslim woman wearing a head covering, there was a Quran in the car, he recognized that she was Arab and Muslim, and despite all that, he shot her.”
Abu Arar left Gaza in 1995. When he returned for a visit years later, after Hamas had seized control of the territory, he says he struggled to recognize the place where he grew up. “I was supposed to stay for three days and I didn’t stay six hours,” he says. “I said: This is not the Gaza I know. I felt like I was inside Iran, inside Tehran.”
Despite his fierce criticism of Hamas, Abu Arar insists on making another distinction. “You can’t say all of Gaza is Hamas,” he says, adding that there are also Gazans who oppose the terrorist organization and that he still receives updates from relatives living there.
A new life he cannot imagine
After October 7, Abu Arar received permanent residency and an Israeli identity card in recognition of his actions. He speaks with deep gratitude about Interior Minister Moshe Arbel, who helped arrange the status. “He stood by me like a man, an incredible man,” Abu Arar says. “I will never forget him, and I will never forget what he did.”
By contrast, he criticizes the policy of home demolitions promoted by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. “It’s not good,” he says. “It creates division, it creates hatred. You can’t constantly talk about coexistence while at the same time playing with people’s emotions.”
Nearly three years after the massacre, relatives and in-laws tell Hamid that it is time to try to build a new life. He even tried. “But it isn’t it,” he says. “I can’t. It is very difficult to accept.”
“They tell me, ‘Hamid, you can’t live like this. Fatma is dead. You have to build a new life, get married.’ I tell them: It’s easy to talk. You can talk until tomorrow.”
Sometimes, he says, he sits alone and searches his memories of Fatma for “one small flaw,” something that might break the perfection with which she remains in his mind. “There isn’t one,” he says. “I’m telling you the truth, there isn’t. A woman like that is what I wish for anyone who wants to live with security, peace and hope.”
He knows Fatma herself would have wanted him to be happy. “But where is that happiness supposed to come from?” he asks. “Only from my children. For them to grow up and study, that is the only happiness I take.”
And that is the promise he intends to keep for her. “Their mother and I promised them they would be educated, and I will continue with that until the last minute of my life,” he says. “I am with them. I don’t leave them for a moment. I have nothing else. This is my family.”

articles.full_text:
PARIS — France test-fired an upgraded version of its M51 strategic ballistic missile from a submarine for the first time on Tuesday, a capability demonstration that President Emmanuel Macron called “very important” for the country’s strategic credibility and which he said would be monitored by allies and adversaries alike.
The nuclear-powered ballistic-missile submarine Le Vigilant fired an M51.3 missile in an acceptance test following the boat’s overhaul, the Ministry of the Armed Forces said in a statement. The missile, which didn’t carry a nuclear warhead, was launched off Finistère in western France and splashed down in the North Atlantic several hundred kilometers from any coastline, the ministry said.
France’s work to upgrade the M51 missile, manufactured by ArianeGroup, is part of a broader modernization of the country’s nuclear deterrence apparatus that also includes the construction of new ballistic-missile submarines and a future upgrade of the Rafale fighter jet that would carry a hypersonic nuclear cruise missile.
“This is a very important moment for our strategic credibility,” Macron told troops onboard a French Navy vessel from which he observed the launch. “Everything that has happened recently and what is happening today will be closely scrutinized by both our allies and our competitors alike, and it already is. Along the course we have set, this is a step forward.”
The modernization of France’s nuclear arsenal comes as the country works with several European allies on what Macron has called “forward deterrence,” a proposal that could involve extending the reach of French nuclear deterrence to those allies, although the details of what that would look like remain vague for now.
Every major overhaul of a French nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine is followed by an acceptance test firing of the M51, the ministry told Defense News in an emailed response to questions.
ArianeGroup and France’s Directorate General for Armament completed a first flight test of the modernized M51 from a launch site in Biscarrosse in southwest France in 2023, and the new missile entered operational service in October last year.
The latest M51.3 variant is estimated to have a range of more than 9,500 kilometers, from more than 9,000 kilometers for the previous version, according to the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists. The missile carries four to six multiple independently-targetable reentry vehicles, or MIRVs, according to the Bulletin.
While the official range of the missile is undisclosed, ArianeGroup says the M51 reaches an altitude of more than 2,000 kilometers before reentering the atmosphere at a speed of Mach 20.
The missile is equipped with the new TNO-2 oceanic nuclear warhead, and offers better performance in terms of range, accuracy and penetration capability, according to the ministry. The solid-propellant three-stage missile weighs more than 50 metric tons, and each of France’s four ballistic missile submarines can carry 16 of them.
“The M51.3 ensures the long-term credibility of the ocean-based component in the face of evolving adversary missile defenses,” the ministry said. “It reflects the commitment of the President of the Republic to maintaining operational credibility of the nuclear forces over the long term, at the level required by the international environment.”
The first version of the M51 was fired from the Biscarrosse launch site in 2006, with the first submarine launch from the SSBN Le Terrible in January 2010. Today’s launch was the seventh time a variant of the M51 was fired from a French submarine, and the 13th launch of the missile overall, all of them “of course, conducted without a nuclear warhead,” according to the ministry.
Rudy Ruitenberg is a Europe correspondent for Defense News. He started his career at Bloomberg News and has experience reporting on technology, commodity markets and politics.

articles.title: The deterrence gap: How can NATO protect its front line from Russia? - Atlantic Council
articles.summary: The deterrence gap: How can NATO protect its front line from Russia?  Atlantic Council
articles.full_text:
Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 challenged much of the common Western understanding of Russia. How can the world better understand Russia? What are the steps forward for Western policy? The Eurasia Center’s “Russia Tomorrow” series seeks to reevaluate conceptions of Russia today and better prepare for its future tomorrow.
Table of contents
These are tense times for NATO’s European frontline states. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is well into its fifth year. US President Donald Trump is reducing troop presence in Europe and questioning America’s commitment to NATO, while the European powers are yet to take on full responsibility for their continent’s security. And the war in the Middle East is consuming finite resources and diverting attention from other security topics.
In this challenging geopolitical environment, it is NATO’s frontline states—especially Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, and Romania that are the focus of this report and are feeling the Kremlin’s threat most acutely. While Finland, Norway, and Turkey similarly share a maritime or land border with Russia, they do not share a Cold War history of being under Moscow’s domination and are not targeted by Russia to the same extent. Russia regularly probes the Baltic states, Poland, and Romania—remaining below the threshold for invoking Article 5, but increasingly employing kinetic means, including drone incursions and sabotage to test their resolve and capacity to respond. This constant atmosphere of intimidation results in psychological pressure on populations, hampers investment, dampens economic outlook, and calls into question NATO’s resolve to deter Russia and other hostile actors.
Geography is key when considering the range of Russian threats and, to a degree, the measures these five eastern flank countries can pursue. Estonia and Latvia share land borders with the Russian Federation proper; and both Lithuania and Poland border Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave and Belarus. Moreover, as Ukraine’s neighbors, Poland and Romania face the spillover effects—including drones and missiles—of Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Land borders with Russia’s de facto satellite state of Belarus constitute a direct military threat since Belarusian territory served as a launch pad for Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion and Belarusian and Russian intelligence services operate in close coordination. Romania borders its closest cultural and linguistic partner, the Republic of Moldova, where the unresolved, Russian-backed conflict in Transnistria poses enduring security risks.
This report examines Russia’s military, cyber, economic, infrastructure, information, and espionage threats to NATO’s eastern flank, and assesses the responses of Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, and Romania. The threats discussed are illustrative rather than exhaustive: The report’s scope does not permit a comprehensive account of Russia’s continuing provocations and operations, and any such catalog would quickly be overtaken by new developments. Nonetheless, with NATO and EU support, as well as regional cooperation, these five frontline states have developed defense strategies across four pillars: military deterrence and territorial defense; strategic communication and societal resilience; cyber defense and critical-infrastructure protection; and counterintelligence to safeguard democratic systems.
The study finds that while conventional military deterrence-building has advanced systematically, measures addressing Russia’s hybrid tactics—particularly in cyber, infrastructure, and information domains—remain more fragmented, under-resourced, and unresolved. Overall, the current response measures do not inspire full societal confidence of frontline states in defense and deterrence capabilities. More significantly, NATO and national responses have largely been reactive and defensive: They have focused on detecting and countering individual provocations but have not built a record of effective deterrence by consistently dissuading Moscow from continuing or escalating them. The prevailing approach remains rooted in a peacetime framework, despite the reality that the frontline security environment increasingly occupies a “gray zone” between peace and war.
The final recommendations offer a critical assessment of the current deterrence record. They argue that frontline states bear a disproportionate and unsustainable burden for safeguarding NATO’s eastern flank, strengthening societal resilience, and deterring Russian aggression and Belarusian involvement. These states therefore require enhanced and sustained support from NATO, the United States, and leading European powers to establish credible deterrence and deliver tangible responses—not merely observation and condemnations—to Russia’s continuing kinetic and hybrid threats. This will require the political will to complement deterrence by denial, which strengthens Allied resilience and closes defensive gaps, with deterrence by punishment: imposing credible and proportionate costs for Russian provocations.
Russia’s threats against NATO’s eastern flank
Russia’s threats against NATO’s eastern flank states are both implicit and explicit, with the former stemming from geography, geopolitics, and Russia’s war in Ukraine and the later involving Russia’s specific operations targeting the five states. These operations can be summed up as the Kremlin’s coordinated hybrid warfare campaign combining military, informational, cyber, and intelligence instruments and seeking to weaken frontline states and the alliance’s resolve to deter Russia. NATO, the European Union, and most Western defense doctrines define hybrid warfare as the coordinated use of military and nonmilitary tools, applied below the threshold of open war, to coerce, destabilize, or weaken a state while maintaining plausible deniability. Over the years Russia had generally maintained its actions just below the Article 5 threshold, while ensuring they are constant enough to shape behavior, resource allocation, and political debate in frontline states. However, recent provocations—whether in drone incursions, infrastructure sabotage, or border violations—have kinetic components. These ambiguities both provide Moscow with deniability of aggression and likewise limit the responses the target states or their allies can or are willing to pursue. The second veil of ambiguity involves the ties between Putin’s and Lukashenko’s regimes and makes it difficult to disentangle the actions of Minsk from those of Moscow.
This report will examine four categories of Russia’s threats with case country examples:
1) Military threats, coercions, and risks.
2) Cyber operations and infrastructure sabotage.
3) Information warfare.
4) Espionage and covert operations.
Military threats, coercions, and risks
Russia’s approach to the Baltic states, Poland, and Romania combines visible military pressure with calibrated kinetic actions designed to remain below the threshold of open war while shaping NATO decision‑making. Military pressures have also reflected the region’s strategic setting. Prior to the 2023 and 2024 accessions of Finland and Sweden to NATO, respectively, the Baltic Sea littoral states faced a more constrained operating environment and a greater prospect of Russian dominance at sea and in the air. Romania anchors NATO’s Black Sea frontage and land access to Ukraine and Moldova, but it is exposed to Russian power projection via the Black Sea and occupied Ukrainian territories.
Russia launched a major force expansion even before 2022, and its military presence and operations near the NATO frontier is an ever-present regional threat. In 2024 Russia recreated the Leningrad Military District and rebuilt the 6th Combined Arms Army and associated corps for operations along NATO’s northeastern flank. Forward‑deployed Russian and Belarusian units near the Suwałki corridor (the narrow border between Poland and Lithuania linking the Baltics to the rest of NATO), Kaliningrad, and the borders of Poland and Lithuania are central to this posture: Kaliningrad hosts the 11th Army Corps and, since late 2025, an expanded 336th Guards Naval Infantry Division. In addition, large Russian‑Belarusian exercises such as the Zapad‑series routinely mobilize forces in the high tens of thousands across the Suwałki–Kaliningrad–Belarus triangle. Estimates suggest that Russia maintains roughly 40,000 ground forces in the wider Baltic theater but could mass up to about 100,000 troops in the region under the guise of exercises, drawing on multiple commands in western Russia.
Russian airspace violations and missile spillover are becoming alarmingly routine. During repeated Russian strikes on Ukraine, Romania has recorded at least eleven drone incursions into its airspace since 2022, including a drone that struck an apartment building in the eastern Romanian city of Galati on May 30, 2026, and a Russian “Shahed” exploded in Moldova on June 13, 2026. Poland has had to scramble jets and temporarily close airports in response to Russian drone swarms and missile penetrations (including cruise missile in July 2026). A drone entered Latvian airspace because of Russian electronic warfare in August 2026, and another one entered Lithuanian airspace in September 2026, prompting NATO fighter jets from Lithuania’s Šiauliai Air Base to shoot it down. These incidents feed public anxiety and force costly readiness measures without crossing the point of an acknowledged “attack” on NATO soil. Belarus has also launched waves of surveillance balloons that have forced nearly routine temporary suspensions of operations at Vilnius airport, showing how low‑cost, deniable tools can generate disproportionate disruption to Lithuanian civilian air traffic and regional security. Across the region, the number of Russian incursions into NATO airspace jumped to eighteen cases in 2025 alone.

However, preparations for this meeting have simultaneously laid bare disagreements over the EU’s role in security matters — and fuelled fears that Brussels’ initiatives will duplicate NATO’s functions, writes Politico.
The publication notes that in recent weeks, ambassadors from all 27 EU countries have met on several occasions to discuss the scenario of such an attack in a so-called ‘restricted format’ – that is, without mobile phones or aides. Diplomats and officials, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the confidential nature of the matter, reported that discussions had intensified following the discovery in August of a drone packed with explosives at Leipzig Airport.
The EU has been discussing such scenarios for several years now, notes Politico. Brussels has developed an ‘anti-hybrid toolkit’ to coordinate responses to cyber-attacks, election interference and acts of sabotage.
However, attention has now shifted to a more serious threat – attacks capable of causing mass casualties. According to two diplomats, it was precisely such scenarios that became the main topic of discussion at last Wednesday’s meeting of EU ambassadors, the publication notes.
According to one EU official, diplomats and ministers are discussing the deployment of emergency response teams, the possibility of allocating a portion of EU funds to the affected country, as well as actions to be taken by the leadership of European institutions in the information sphere.
‘The situation could become complicated’
However, discussions at EU level have already caused irritation in some capitals. There, it is felt that the European Union is overstepping its role in the security sphere and risks duplicating the key functions of NATO — the transatlantic alliance that has been the mainstay of European security for 80 years now.
“For decision-makers at all levels, the situation could prove very confusing,” said Oana Lungescu, former NATO spokesperson and now a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute for Defence Studies. “If confusion or duplication of functions arises, decision-making may be slowed down. And this is fraught with consequences, as in such situations time is of the essence.”
There is another problem: the EU lacks a secure communications system, and diplomats therefore fear that the confidential information they exchange at meetings could be leaked.
The criticism has emerged against the backdrop of attempts by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to strengthen the EU’s position on security.
In her latest State of the Union address in Strasbourg, the former German defence minister proposed establishing an ‘emergency security protocol’ that would allow EU countries to coordinate their actions in situations such as the one currently under discussion. According to two diplomats, this protocol, like von der Leyen’s proposal to establish a ‘European Security Council’, will form part of the new ‘European Security Strategy’, which is due to be presented in early November.
However, some diplomats have spoken out against the idea. In their view, it would take months to set up new mechanisms, and these might duplicate existing EU structures.
Rather than creating new frameworks and further overburdening the system, one senior national diplomat suggested utilising existing crisis response tools.
“We are very concerned about this emergency security protocol,” Politico quotes the diplomat as saying. “We already have all the necessary mechanisms in place. In the event of a crisis, there is the Integrated Political Crisis Response (IPCR) mechanism, which proved its worth during the pandemic and other crises.”
The IPCR mechanism, established under the Treaty of Lisbon, allows the country holding the rotating EU presidency to convene an emergency meeting, at the request of an affected state, involving experts from NATO, the UN and other international organisations.

New Delhi presents a strategic ceasefire framework for Eastern Europe
India has officially outlined a specific three-part ceasefire strategy to stop hostilities between Moscow and Kyiv. Foreign Minister S Jaishankar delivered this proposal directly to Ukrainian officials during his recent visit to Eastern Europe. The framework prioritizes stopping direct strikes on energy facilities, ensuring safe passage for commercial ships, and maintaining uninterrupted grain shipments through Black Sea ports.
International diplomatic efforts
Diplomatic sources confirm that Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha recognized this initiative as the most detailed among current international efforts. Other nations, including Egypt, Turkey, and the United States, have also submitted separate negotiation options. Egypt and Turkey primarily target agricultural exports, while American negotiators concentrate on halting power grid attacks. New Delhi combined these critical elements into one unified document to address multiple humanitarian concerns simultaneously.
Changing role in global mediation
Russian President Vladimir Putin recently praised Prime Minister Narendra Modi for offering practical ideas to reach a mutually acceptable resolution. Putin specifically highlighted India's neutral diplomatic position throughout the five-year conflict.
Global observers note that this geopolitical crisis has severely disrupted global supply chains since early 2022. By presenting a concrete framework, Indian diplomats are shifting from simple advocacy to active negotiation. Jaishankar reinforced this evolving position during the Munich Security Conference in Delhi, confirming ongoing practical discussions with both sides. Both warring nations continue evaluating the exact terms. Ukrainian leaders remain open to different negotiation formats. However, they insist any final agreement must protect their critical port infrastructure alongside pausing direct frontline combat operations. New Delhi will likely maintain regular contact with both capitals to refine the proposed steps over the coming weeks.

articles.summary: Politico: Save yourself! Putin doesn't care if it's the EU or NATO  EADaily
articles.full_text:
Although it is not known for certain about any hostile actions of Russia, the authorities of the EU countries are preparing to repel a "major hybrid attack", regularly scaring residents of their countries. However, the preparation has already exposed disagreements — there are fears that Brussels' initiatives will duplicate NATO's functions, writes the globalist resource Politico.
In recent weeks, the ambassadors of all 27 countries The EU has repeatedly met to discuss the scenario of such an attack in the so—called limited format - that is, without phones and without assistants. Diplomats and officials on condition of anonymity due to the confidentiality of the topic reported that discussions intensified after a drone packed with explosives was found at Leipzig airport in August.
Similar scenarios The EU has been discussing it for years. Brussels has developed an "anti-hybrid toolkit" to coordinate responses to cyber attacks, election interference and sabotage. However, now attention has shifted to a more serious threat — attacks fraught with mass casualties. According to the two diplomats, such scenarios became the main topic of the ambassadors' meeting. The EU last Wednesday.
The EU claims that after the start of the Russian special operation on In Ukraine, Moscow has allegedly intensified a campaign of cyber attacks, sabotage and other covert operations throughout the bloc.
"European democracies are facing increasing threats," Justice Commissioner Michael McGrath told Politico. "We are strengthening our threat forecasting and detection capabilities, improving early warning systems, and providing Europe with the ability to respond quickly and together if the resilience of our democracy is suddenly put to the test."
According to one of the EU officials, diplomats and ministers are discussing the deployment of emergency response teams, the possibility of allocating part of the EU funds to the affected country, as well as actions by the leadership of European institutions in the information field.
"We have to be ready for something really serious," said one senior EU diplomat. —Alas, Leipzig has shown that a very serious incident with numerous victims cannot be considered incredible."
Another official The EU added:
"Given the scope and scale of Russia's actions, sooner or later casualties are inevitable. We've just been incredibly lucky so far that it hasn't happened yet."
The European Union is faced with almost daily reports of so—called hybrid attacks - so EU and NATO calls subversion below the threshold of a direct military attack. On Tuesday, Bulgarian authorities reported that several sailors were missing after their ship sank in the Black Sea as a result of a drone attack.
Prior to that, there was an incident at Leipzig Airport, a suspicious fire at a Polish ground station providing Starlink communications, as well as an attempt to organize arson attacks on commercial vehicles in the countries EU and UK. All this is accompanied by regular violations of airspace.
"It is quite obvious that as Russia moves to more and more lethal means, testing our readiness and determination to take retaliatory measures, victims will inevitably appear at some point," said Teja Tiilikainen, director of the European Center of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats. "Sooner or later, intentionally or accidentally, that's where it ends."
If several citizens of the countries die as a result of the attack The EU or NATO, both organizations will be expected to take decisive action.
"We are very afraid that at some point the lives of allies will be lost," said one of the NATO diplomats.
After that, according to him, the "pressure" to act will become "very high." However, discussions at the level of The EU has already annoyed some capitals. They believe that the European Union is going beyond its role in the security sphere and risks duplicating the key functions of NATO — the transatlantic alliance, which has been the pillar of European security for 80 years.
"For decision—makers at all levels, the situation can be very confusing," said Oana Lungescu, a former NATO spokeswoman and now an honored researcher at the Royal United Institute for Defense Studies. — If there is confusion or duplication of functions, decision-making may slow down. And this is fraught with consequences, because in such situations time decides everything."
There is another problem: the EU does not have a secure communications system, and therefore diplomats are afraid of "drains" of confidential information that they exchange at meetings. These concerns only intensified after reports that the former Hungarian Foreign Minister conveyed to his Russian counterpart the content of the talks at the leadership level. As a result, the capitals began to limit the transfer of classified information to the NATO format.
"My Government is very suspicious of the exchange of secret intelligence in The Committee of Permanent Representatives to the EU or even at meetings of leaders," said a diplomat from one of the eastern flank countries. — It either pops up in The media, or immediately goes to Moscow."
Criticism sounded against the background of attempts by the President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen to strengthen the position The EU in the field of security. In his last speech on the state of the European Union in Strasbourg, the former German Defense minister proposed creating an "emergency security protocol" that would allow EU countries to coordinate actions in situations like the one currently being discussed. According to the two diplomats, this protocol, as well as von der Leyen's proposal to create a "European Security Council", will be included in the new "European Security Strategy", which is scheduled to be presented in early November.
However, some diplomats opposed it. In their opinion, it will take months to create new mechanisms, and they themselves can duplicate existing EU structures. Instead of creating new formats and overloading the system even more, one of the high-ranking national diplomats suggested using the existing anti-crisis response tools.
"We are very concerned about this emergency security protocol," the diplomat said. "We already have all the necessary mechanisms. In the event of a crisis, there is an Integrated Political Response Mechanism (IPCR), which has performed very well in a pandemic and during other crises."
The IPCR mechanism, created within the framework of the Lisbon Treaty, allows the EU presidency on a rotating basis, at the request of the affected state, to convene an emergency meeting with the participation of experts from NATO, the UN and other international organizations. In the event of a major hybrid attack, it is the affected country that will have to decide how to proceed. After the terrorist attacks in the Bataclan Concert Hall in Paris in 2015, France invoked Article 42.7 of the EU Treaty — and this is the only case of applying the provision on mutual assistance. However, as Lungescu notes, this was a "purely political" decision by Paris, which did not lead to large-scale practical measures of mutual assistance, apart from coordinating investigations of terrorist attacks between France and Belgium.
In order to avoid confusion about who is responsible for what in the event of a mass casualty attack, Lungescu proposes a clear division of roles: NATO should be engaged in intelligence sharing and military deterrence, and the EU in civilian response.
According to Tiilikainen, efforts The EU's efforts to coordinate the response to hybrid attacks are certainly useful, but have their limits. At the same time, she stressed that they cannot be compared with measures to strengthen resilience at the national level, such as the Finnish approach to ensuring "comprehensive security." Lungescu also stressed that Moscow sees no fundamental difference between the two organizations.
"Frankly speaking, President Putin does not care whether decisions are made in The Committee of Permanent Representatives or at the level of the North Atlantic Alliance," she said, referring to the ambassadors' meetings. The EU and the governing body of NATO. "Moscow thinks differently."

articles.title: The Two Africas
articles.summary: Who will benefit from the continent's investment boom?
articles.full_text:
Last year, U.S. President Donald Trump told a group of African leaders that the United States would be “shifting from aid to trade.” Washington had already begun to close USAID, the world’s biggest development agency, and many U.S. allies followed suit, cutting their own aid programs in Africa.
Amid the humanitarian cuts, however, international business interest in Africa is growing. The continent possesses huge reserves of the critical minerals the world needs. Foreign investors are eyeing Africa’s young workforce, growing consumer base, and ports located along vital global trade routes. And competition among China, the United States, Europe, India, and the Gulf states is bringing a wider array of investors than ever before. This year, roughly half of the world’s 20 fastest-growing economies are likely to be African.
Yet these gains won’t be distributed evenly across the continent. Many countries are too unstable, underdeveloped, or corrupt to attract foreign capital and will likely stay trapped in stagnation. But the ones that attract sustained outside investment and cultivate their domestic economies could see tremendous growth—and have a chance to follow the industrialization models that turned Singapore, South Korea, and Taiwan into leading markets in the twentieth century. Those African countries that undertake sustained reforms might prosper long enough to provide vast new opportunities for their people and accrue real geopolitical power.
AFTER AID
Africa remains a relatively small player in the global economy. It makes up about 20 percent of the world’s population but accounts for just three percent of GDP and three percent of global trade. Over the past quarter century, foreign direct investment across sub-Saharan Africa has remained relatively flat—around two to three percent as a share of GDP—and most of it has gone to extracting oil, diamonds, and gold and other minerals.
But certain countries and regions are growing quickly. Take southern Africa, which has relatively good interstate infrastructure and low barriers to trade, although many nontariff barriers still exist. Twelve countries in southern Africa have a power pool that connects their grids and allows them to buy and sell electricity among one another, leading to greater efficiency and reliability. The region is also home to the world’s oldest running customs union—made up of Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia, and South Africa. The five countries coordinate trade policy, share customs revenue, and implement a common external tariff. Mature freight and logistics networks increasingly connect the mineral belts in the continent’s southern center to ports on both African coasts. These institutions do not fully eliminate the difficulties of doing business across borders, but they allow investors to think in terms of regional rather than merely national markets. Reforms and efforts to connect are paying off in this part of the continent: Botswana and Zambia are set to grow by 4.7 and 4.3 percent this year, respectively.
Further north, Nigeria, with its vast entrepreneurial ecosystem and growing interest from investors, gives West Africa huge market scale. Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda form an increasingly valuable East African commercial core. Some smaller African states are thriving: the island nation of Mauritius has developed into an international financial center. Botswana and Rwanda have attracted investment by providing stable policymaking environments, making up for limited scale.
The continent as a whole also has enormous opportunities on its horizon. Favorable demography gives many African countries a potential advantage. As advanced economies grow old in the coming decades, African countries will see much of their population mature into working age. As the demographer Nicholas Eberstadt noted in these pages in 2024, “By 2040, national cohorts of people between the ages of 15 and 49 will decrease more or less everywhere outside sub-Saharan Africa.” Urbanization presents a similar opportunity. According to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, nearly two out of every three Africans will be living in cities by 2050. A richer, more urban African population would attract investment well beyond the extractive industries that have typically dominated foreign capital inflows; Africa’s young population has already made enormous advances in areas such as financial technology and the democratization of financial services.
 Foreign governments are racing to gain access to African harbors.
Africa also still has many of the resources that the rest of the world needs. Sub-Saharan Africa is home to 30 percent of the known reserves of critical minerals. China recognized the strategic significance of these resources early and has spent decades building a near monopoly over the critical mineral industry in many parts of Africa. Nearly all sub-Saharan African countries have signed on to Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative, the biggest global infrastructure project in modern history, which has funded African trade corridors such as the Addis Ababa–Djibouti and Mombasa-Nairobi railways. China’s overall investment in the continent over the last 20 years has exceeded $350 billion, and Beijing has recently transitioned from a chief lender to a top debt collector in the developing world.
Now the United States and its partners are hoping to make more inroads. Last year, the Trump administration announced deals to secure American access to minerals in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda at the same time as it unveiled a deal meant to secure peace between the two countries. The United States and other G-7 countries have backed projects such as the Lobito Corridor, a rail line linking the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zambia to Angola’s Atlantic coast. When complete, these new lines will transport vast quantities of copper, a metal used in solar panels, heat pumps, batteries, and electric vehicles. The United States also recently extended the African Growth and Opportunity Act, which grants sub-Saharan countries duty-free access to American markets through 2028.
Africa’s geography also puts it in a position to compete in global trade networks. Two of the world’s most strategic maritime chokepoints, the Suez Canal and the Bab el Mandeb Strait, are bordered by African shores. Attacks by the Houthis, the Yemeni rebel group, on commercial shipping in the Red Sea over the last three years have pushed major carriers around the Cape of Good Hope, boosting traffic at ports along Africa’s southern and western coasts. Foreign governments are also racing to gain access to African harbors. Chinese state-owned enterprises have built, financed, or operated at least 78 ports across 32 African countries. Turkey manages the one in Mogadishu and has opened up the largest overseas Turkish military base nearby, where it trains Somali forces. Emirati companies operate ports in more than a dozen countries.
Perhaps the most underappreciated commercial development in Africa has been the recent influx of Gulf capital. Gulf states look to the continent for arable land, critical minerals, political influence, and diversified trade routes. The United Arab Emirates has become, by some measures, Africa’s single largest source of new foreign direct investment, committing nearly $110 billion between 2019 and 2023—even outspending China in some years. Similarly, Saudi Arabia and Qatar deploy sovereign capital into real estate, mining, and digital infrastructure. Gulf sovereign wealth funds, with patient capital and the capacity to move quickly on commercial timelines, are appealing partners. At a time when Chinese lending is dwindling in many places, Gulf states are filling the void. And many African governments prefer the Gulf model, in which investors tend to take equity in a project rather than saddling the borrowing state with debt.
A TALE OF TWO CONTINENTS
This outside interest, however, does not mean that every African country can benefit from it. For African governments, the question is whether they can convert this new race for minerals into durable economic growth and material gains for ordinary people. Continental statistics obscure enormous variation. Over 80 percent of foreign direct investment in Africa is concentrated in just 15 countries, according to the United Nations.
Investors can tolerate many kinds of difficulties. They have less tolerance for uncertainty about whether contracts, regulations, or governments will remain stable long enough for an investment to pay off. Military governments that came to power in coups in Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger between 2020 and 2023 have drastically changed their countries’ economic landscapes and, worse, created enormous instability and hardship for local populations. Madagascar’s coup last year halted oversight of and reforms to the economy. In many jurisdictions, such as Egypt and Mozambique, sovereign debt distress or the risk of it leaves little fiscal room for other government spending.
A similar distinction applies to Africa’s urbanization and its demographic potential. Currently, big cities including Abidjan, Dar es Salaam, Johannesburg, Lagos, and Nairobi punch below their weight economically because they are cut off from one another by inefficient customs regimes, poor infrastructure, and incompatible payment systems. Population growth by itself cannot generate economic returns at a continental scale. And as the South African writer Jakkie Cilliers argued in these pages, Africa’s youth bulge will only be an asset if young people in the coming decades have access to education, formal employment, and functioning institutions. Otherwise, unemployed young people can become a source of instability.
